andersen-improvisatore-howitt-1847:
Hans Christian Andersen published The Improvisatore in Denmark in 1835, and Mary Howitt Englished it in 1847. The novel made Andersen famous across Europe a decade before his fairy tales ruled nurseries. Antonio, a poor Roman boy with a gift for improvised song, tells his own story from childhood onward.

Antonio rises from street singer to admired performer, through love, loss, and patronage. Rome, Naples, and Venice glow in the background of his fortunes. Andersen drew on his own Italian travels and his hunger for recognition. Howitt, a tireless carrier of Scandinavian writing into English, gave the book its English life. It stands apart from the tales, as his great novel of the artist.
arxiv-2512-00047:
Angelina Parfenova, Alexander Denzler, and Juergen Pfeffer study how language model agents converge when they annotate data together. Models are more and more deployed in shared settings, yet their teamwork as black-box agents is little understood. The team simulated thousands of multi-agent, multi-round talks on an inductive coding task.

The runs produced well over a hundred thousand messages, capturing final labels and full interaction records. Watching settling unfold shows whether agreement reflects shared understanding or mere herding. That gap matters for using agent panels as research assistants. Full records are preserved in the data, so settling can be studied as a process, not just an outcome.
arxiv-2512-00547:
Rebuilding a moving scene in three dimensions is much harder when several people interact with objects at once. Sandika Biswas, Qianyi Wu, Biplab Banerjee, and Hamid Rezatofighi present asset-driven semantic reconstruction of dynamic scenes in 2025. The scenes involve multiple humans and their complex interactions with surroundings.

Such environments matter for augmented and virtual reality, gaming, and embodied AI, yet they remain underexplored. Diverse motion patterns and frequent occlusions defeat simpler reconstruction pipelines. An asset-driven approach, reusing known object models inside the scene, could keep reconstructions stable even when people block the camera's view. Asset-driven means known objects are fitted into the scene rather than rebuilt from scratch.
arxiv-2512-00647:
Vision Mamba models promise transformer-level skill with lower cost, yet their efficiency is capped by the number of image tokens. Shanhui Liu, Rui Xu, and Yunke Wang present MambaScope in 2025, a coarse-to-fine scoping method for efficient vision Mamba. Token pruning and merging cut computation but lose information.

Discarding or compressing token representations throws away detail that fine recognition may need. A scoping approach first surveys the image coarsely, then spends tokens where detail matters. Keeping information while cutting cost would widen where state-space vision models can run, from medical scanners to mobile cameras. Coarse-to-fine mirrors how people scan a scene before examining details. Vision Mamba's promise is efficiency, so a method that protects it is on theme.
arxiv-2512-00747:
Tingjun Zhang and a large team of physicists study a magnetic material called alpha-MnTe in a 2025 paper. The material is a semiconducting altermagnet, a magnet with no net moment that still splits electron behavior by spin. The team adds lithium to it and watches what changes.

Using inelastic neutron scattering, they bounce neutrons off the material to probe its inner motions. Adding lithium flips the spin direction from in-plane to out-of-plane. It also raises the density of mobile charge carriers. The evidence points to an interplay between those roaming carriers and local magnetic moments, which shapes how the material acts.
arxiv-2512-00947:
Liyao Li and a large team study how language models can treat tables as a data type of their own in a 2025 paper. Tables run much of the world's stored data, in spreadsheets, databases, and reports. Language models shine on plain text, so researchers have worked to extend them to table reasoning tasks.

Their paper presents tables as a modality, a distinct channel like text or image that a model must learn to read. Rows, columns, and cell relations carry meaning that plain text flattens away. Framing tables this way guides how models should encode and reason over them. Better table skills matter for finance, science, and business tools.
arxiv-2512-01047:
Tanmay Ambadkar, Đorđe Žikelić, and Abhinav Verma automate the sharpening of learning specs in a 2025 paper. Logical specifications can guide reinforcement learning agents toward complex tasks by stating rules the behavior must satisfy. When a spec is under-specified, though, it leaves too much open, and agents may fail to learn useful policies.

The authors explore improving coarse-grained specs through an exploration-guided strategy. The agent's own exploration reveals which parts of the spec need refinement. Automating that loop could save the hand-tuning that now limits spec-based training. Better specs mean agents that learn intended behavior, not loopholes.
arxiv-2512-01347:
Fukunaga, Nakatsuyama, and Takahashi study odd points on translation surfaces. A translation surface sweeps one curve along another. Points where the surface pinches or folds are called singular. Past work dealt with the case where the two curves are freely set.

Here the pair handle the linked case, where the curves rest on each other. They use framed surface theory to sort the odd points. The work wraps up the full study of such surfaces. A full sort helps in geometry and in design of curved forms for art and building. The framed view sorts pinches, folds, and cusps by local form, giving each odd point a name tied to how it can unfold.
arxiv-2512-01447:
Maya Sadeler Perrin and co-authors study Hawkes processes with a drifting baseline. Hawkes processes model events that spark more events. Their baseline rate is often fixed. In brain, social, and finance data, outside factors drift over time and move that baseline.

The team lets a diffusion process drive the baseline. They study long-run acts, inference, and tests for the new class. The model spans many variables at once. It should fit event data where a slow hidden drift shapes bursts, like trades or nerve spikes. Diffusion-driven baselines also absorb seasonality, since slow outside cycles enter through the same drift term that carries trends and shocks.
arxiv-2512-01547:
Muratore and co-authors study Bootes I, a very faint dwarf galaxy, with space telescopes. Such dwarfs are old and poor in metals. Their metal spread is a fossil record of early star birth. It tests models of first stars and dark matter halos.

Data from JWST and Hubble map stars in the dwarf. The team reads the spread of metals across its stars. They also hunt for binary stars in the system. Those reads sharpen the tale of how the smallest galaxies formed and how their first stars enriched them. Binary counts matter too, since unseen companions can fake a wider metal spread if their light blends with the star being gauged.
arxiv-2512-01647:
Andrea Coccaro and co-authors learn to rebuild muon tracks at the LHC. Charged particle paths must be rebuilt with high precision. Good tracks need sharp hit picks and mass momentum gauges. Errors there blur all later physics results.

Their differentiable approach learns the rebuild step itself. It can be tuned end to end for final accuracy. Muons are clean probes of new physics at colliders. Sharper muon tracks lift searches for rare decays and new particles that show up first as small track shifts. End-to-end tuning also spots which hits hurt most, guiding detector crews toward the sensor flaws that cost the most physics reach.
arxiv-2512-01747:
Aguasca-Cabot and the LST-1 team report follow-up views of the brightest gamma-ray burst ever seen. GRB 221009A was detected in October 2022. Part of its brightness came from its close distance. That closeness makes it a unique lab for burst physics.

The LST-1 telescope chased its high-energy afterglow. Such follow-ups test how jets cool and spread after the blast. A record-bright event lets weak traits show that dim bursts hide. Results refine models of the most violent explosions known in the cosmos. Cherenkov telescopes catch the highest energies, where burst jets may hide a second component that satellite data alone cannot resolve.
arxiv-2512-02147:
EP240222a is the first tidal disruption by an intermediate-mass black hole caught in real time, with multi-wavelength observations and spectroscopic confirmation. Wenkai Li and a large team present in 2025 a five-stage model explaining why its light curves broke the usual theoretical expectations.

In their picture, the shredded star's stream circles inefficiently, meets the forming disk late, and its light is reprocessed before escaping. Each stage leaves a mark on the evolving brightness that the model reproduces. Intermediate-mass black holes are the missing link between stellar and supermassive ones, so a well-explained first event anchors a new observational field.
arxiv-2512-02347:
When many users want the same popular file from one transmitter, sending it once by multicast beats sending it user by user, but users must cooperate. Anjali Yadav and four co-authors use cooperative game theory in 2025 to find when users gain by forming coalitions for multicast reception.

A coalition can share the costs and benefits of joining a multicast group, and game theory predicts which groupings are stable. The framework of coalitional games lets the authors state precise incentive conditions. Multicast efficiency matters more as wireless traffic grows, and understanding users' incentives decides whether cooperative schemes survive outside theory.
arxiv-2512-02447:
Spiking neural networks promise brain-like, energy-sipping computation, but their object detectors often waste their temporal gift by feeding neurons nearly identical inputs at every step. Fan Luo and four co-authors add a Temporal Dynamics Enhancer in 2025 for directly trained spiking object detectors.

Conventional designs replicate the input or stack it into fixed-interval frames, flattening the time structure the spikes could exploit. Enhancing temporal dynamics gives neurons varied, informative stimulation across steps. Better spiking detectors would bring accurate vision to power-starved devices, from drones to wearable cameras.
arxiv-2512-02847:
Theodoros Katsoulas and Kyriakos Tamvakis test how the early universe might have inflated inside Einstein-Cartan gravity. Their theory lets the action depend on two curvature measures: the Ricci scalar and the Holst invariant. Einstein-Cartan gravity adds torsion, a twist of spacetime, to the usual picture.

The models studied add cubic terms of the Holst invariant to the action. The authors examine the inflationary behavior those terms produce. Viable inflation inside modified gravity widens the options for explaining the universe's smooth, flat start, and future sky surveys can test them. Twist in space time is a bold add on. The early sky is the one place such a bold move can be tried and judged.
arxiv-2512-02947:
Samuel Andrello, Daniel Alabi, and Simon J. L. Billinge organize how inorganic materials are made so machines can predict full recipes. Machine learning now predicts new materials with novel properties quickly. Working out how to synthesize those materials remains largely unsolved, though.

Earlier work predicted precursors or conditions, rarely the whole synthesis pathway. The authors present a graphical framework and datasets that represent full reactions. Structured pathways let models learn from real lab history, moving prediction from what to make toward how to make it in an actual laboratory. Full paths, not just parts, are what a lab tech must run at the bench. Data in path form meets the tech where the work is done each day.
arxiv-2512-03247:
AI image edits often leave seams and color shifts. Haitian Zheng and co-authors present PixPerfect to fix those flaws in this 2025 work. Latent diffusion models raised edit quality, but their compression can cause pixel-level mismatches at edit borders.

Past fixes often fail to remove all artifacts or do not transfer across models. The authors add a pixel-space refinement step guided by a discriminative check. Seamless edits matter for photo work, design, and film. A method that works across latent types would be widely useful. Pixel-level polish decides whether an edit looks real at a glance, especially along hair and edges.
arxiv-2512-03347:
Robots learning to handle objects often drift off course. William van den Bogert, Gregory Linkowski, and Nima Fazeli present GrOMP to fix that in this 2025 work. Imitation learning copies expert moves, but small errors compound and hurt precision.

GrOMP projects the grasped object back onto a lower-dimensional manifold, a constrained surface of valid poses. Keeping a loosely held object on that surface limits error growth. The method targets repetitive tasks like industrial assembly. More precise imitation could make robot training faster and safer. Manifold projection acts during learning, correcting drift before errors compound into failure.
arxiv-2512-03547:
Mixed-integer programs are powerful but slow to solve exactly. Stefan Clarke and Bartolomeo Stellato propose a learning-based hierarchy in this 2025 work. Such programs model scheduling, logistics, and design problems with both whole and continuous choices.

Their architecture splits the original problem into higher and lower level problems. Both are smaller, so solutions come faster while staying high in quality. Learning guides the split for structured problems. Faster mixed-integer solving could improve planning in transport, energy, and manufacturing. Hierarchy also lets planners refine only the hard parts of a schedule.
arxiv-2512-03947:
Training a support vector machine means running an optimisation algorithm, and knowing when to stop is worth money at scale. Matthew Hough and Stephen A. Vavasis analyse that stopping problem in a 2025 preprint. Their core idea: stop not at a fixed accuracy, but when the current classifier is certified to agree with the optimal one on points that matter.

For a perturbed SVM formulation, they derive a stopping condition that certifies points correctly classified by both classifiers, with no assumptions on the data at all. Under a geometric model of two clean clusters plus noise, certifying one point can guarantee the whole well-behaved set is separated. They add computable bounds for two algorithms, FISTA and coordinate descent. The analysis exposes flaws in the stopping rule of the popular LIBLINEAR package, which can stop too early or too late.
arxiv-2512-04047:
Persuasion used to be expensive, so political elites could shape public opinion only crudely, through schools and mass media. Nadav Kunievsky asks what changes when artificial intelligence makes persuasion cheap and precise, in a 2025 economics preprint. In his dynamic model, elites deliberately choose how far to reshape how policy preferences are distributed, paying persuasion costs and needing majority support.

With a single elite in charge, optimal intervention tends to push opinion toward polarised profiles. The author calls this drift the polarization pull, and better persuasion technology speeds it up. With two opposed elites alternating in power, incentives flip in places: each side may park society in cohesive semi-lock regions that rivals struggle to overturn. Depending on the setting, cheaper persuasion can then heighten or dampen polarisation. Polarisation, on this account, becomes a designed instrument of governance.
arxiv-2601-06647:
Krishna Vinod and co-authors present eSkiTB in 2026, a synthetic event-based dataset. Its purpose is tracking skiers, a hard vision problem. Tracking in RGB broadcast footage faces motion blur and clutter.

Static overlays also obscure the fast-moving athlete in broadcasts. Event cameras sense contrast changes asynchronously, avoiding many such artifacts. Yet a controlled benchmark for winter-sport tracking has been missing. Their synthetic dataset fills that gap for event-based tracking research. Synthetic data lets researchers vary conditions that broadcasts fix arbitrarily. Ski speed, lighting, and background can be controlled in generation. Vision readers get a new testbed for event cameras in sports. It may guide real broadcast analytics for winter events later.
arxiv-2601-06847:
Mengmeng Zhang and four co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on vision-language models in medicine. Such models can write smooth, clear text about a scan or a photo. Yet they often fail to point to the spot in the image that backs up their words.

The authors trace that flaw to a lack of good training pairs. Few sets link a phrase in text to the right spot in a medical image. To fill the gap, they built MedGround. MedGround is a tool chain that turns mask data into pairs of text and image spots. The pairs are checked, so teams can train models to ground their claims in what they see.
arxiv-2601-07147:
Ji He wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on hidden wireless links that must stay unseen. The setup uses a system called PASS. A set of wardens watch the air for signs of a link. The wardens are spread out, and each one makes a yes-or-no call on what it hears. The calls are then merged by a majority vote.

The link in view sends data down to a user. At the same time, it sends random noise to hide the link's trace. The design uses two waveguides at once. One path bears the data, and the other bears the noise. He tests three laws for how PASS spreads its power. The laws are named as general, proportional, and equal. The goal is a link that works while the wardens, as a group, fail to spot that it is there at all.
arxiv-2601-07547:
Wentu Song, Kui Cai, and Tony Q. S. Quek study how many damaged copies are needed to rebuild a sequence exactly. The setting is the Levenshtein sequence reconstruction problem. A sequence passes through a channel that deletes one symbol and substitutes two others. Several erroneous copies arrive at the receiver. The question is the minimum number of copies that guarantees correct reconstruction.

Answers to this question set the redundancy needed in storage and communication systems. DNA-based data storage faces exactly these deletion and substitution errors. Knowing the threshold tells engineers when reconstruction is possible in principle. The authors work on the single-deletion, two-substitution channel as a clean test case. The paper serves coding theorists and storage system designers. It adds one precise piece to the broader reconstruction theory.
arxiv-2601-07647:
Caspar Schauß and colleagues examine a blind spot in studies of pit thermal energy storage. A pit store is a large lined hole filled with hot water, used with district heating. It adds flexibility on both daily and seasonal scales. Most large energy system studies, the authors note, ignore temperature differences between the store and the network.

Their setting is a sector-coupled energy system with high-temperature district heating. Sector coupling links electricity, heat, and transport in one model. When network and storage temperatures differ, usable stored energy changes. Ignoring that gap can distort plans for storage size and operation. The paper speaks to energy modelers who design heating systems for renewable-heavy grids. It argues for temperature detail in models that guide real investment.
arxiv-2601-08247: Liu He builds reinforcement learning agents that carry human cognitive biases into financial trading. The 2026 arXiv paper notes that markets reflect behavior that deviates from full rationality. Standard reinforcement learning models assume rational agents and may miss psychological effects. He integrates cognitive biases into the learning framework for trading decisions. The hypothesis is that biased agents can show human-like trading behavior. A second hope is better risk-adjusted returns than standard agents achieve. The study serves readers at the join of behavioral finance and machine learning.
arxiv-2601-08747:
Rubing Chen and four co-authors ask when a smart system should look facts up, and when it should just think. Many systems now fetch text at each step to help them solve hard tasks. That habit costs time and power. It can also fill the work space with text that does not help, and scores can drop.

The team builds an agent that learns to choose. At each step it can fetch new text, or it can reason with what it has. The aim is to grow the work context in a wise way, not by force. A reader gets a plan for AI help that is both cheaper to run and less prone to noise from poor search hits.
arxiv-2601-08847:
JV Roig sets out a new way to grade AI tools that fetch facts. Old tests use fixed asks and fixed right replies. Such tests can leak into train sets, so scores rise with no real gain. Human made right replies also cost much and can hold bias. Roig flips the task on its head to dodge all three flaws.

His method is called RIKER. It first builds a fake world where all facts are known by design. It then makes texts from those facts, and asks drawn from them. Since the truth was set first, grading is cheap and firm. A reader who grades fetch tools gets a repeat plan. It can make fresh tests that no train set has seen.
arxiv-2601-09747:
Marcílio Ferreira dos Santos and Cleiton de Lima Ricardo map dengue in Recife, Brazil, with tools from physics. Their 2026 arXiv paper covers reported cases from 2015 to 2024. Cases are treated as point clouds in space, and their connectivity is tracked across scales.

The authors use Vietoris-Rips filtrations and zero-dimensional persistent homology. Those tools watch clusters of cases merge as the scale grows. The multi-scale view reveals in detail how the city's many cases organize and connect. Patterns of spread can guide where mosquito control teams and clinics will do the most good.
arxiv-2601-10147:
Mei-Qi Gao and co authors ask if noise can calm chaos in light based rigs. Past work on chaos in such rigs used a mean field view. That view takes the rig as smooth and free of noise. It is a clean but fake case.

Chaos is quick to grow from small shifts. Even tiny noise can blow up in time. That puts the clean view in doubt. The team adds real noise to the rig. They find that noise can quench the chaos. The rig then acts in a more tame way than the clean view would say.
arxiv-2601-10247:
S. Ghinescu and S. Stoica update key counts for double beta decay hunts. In this decay, a core sheds two electrons at once. Hunts for a rare form of it may prove new physics. To plan a hunt, labs need exact counts for how the electrons share energy.

Those counts are named phase space factors. The team also give the full energy hues and how the pair's paths link. Fresh counts help labs tune their gear for the best catch. They also help labs tell one decay form from the next. The work is a ref update for the field.
arxiv-2601-10647:
Guido De Philippis and Alessandro Pigati work on the Michael-Simon inequality, a tool from geometric analysis. The classic version deals with area, the isotropic energy of a surface. They study energies that depend on direction, called anisotropic. Such energies arise when a material's cost varies with how a surface is tilted.

Their functional adds up a direction-based weight over a surface's tangent planes. They prove bounds for energies close to plain area. The proof leans on multilinear Kakeya-type bounds, deep results about how tubes can overlap. The paper links two fields that rarely meet. Its methods may help analysts treat a wider class of surface energies.
arxiv-2601-10747:
Silke K. Kaiser evaluates how to place traffic sensors across a city's streets. Planners need traffic volumes for every street segment to guide urban policy and greener mobility. Sensors are pricey to install and keep up, so only some streets have them. The rest of the network's volumes must be filled in from those readings.

Kaiser's data-driven study asks which sensor layouts make that fill-in most trustworthy. Placement choices made early lock in years of data quality. A poor layout leaves blind spots where policy flies dark. The work speaks to city governments that must stretch a sensor budget across a whole street network.
arxiv-2601-10947:
Anders Høst-Madsen studies faithful simulation of broadcast measurements in a quantum setting. A central server, Charlie, holds a quantum system and measures it with a general POVM. Two others, Alice and Bob, each care only about a partial function of Charlie's outcome. The question is how Charlie's single measurement can be shared so both get what they need.

The setup captures a common pattern: one measurement, many partial readers. Faithful simulation asks when the partial results can be produced without loss. The answer bears on quantum networks where measurement data are precious. It also touches the theory of how quantum information can be split among parties with different interests.
arxiv-2601-11147:
Zixu Wang, Bingbing Xu, Yige Yuan, Huawei Shen, and Xueqi Cheng rethink agentic workflow generation for multi-agent systems. Such systems solve tasks by coordinating agents through workflows. Workflows can be generated per task or per query. Query-level generation tailors each run, but its costs and benefits against task-level design were unclear. The authors analyze both, with theory and experiments.

They find that query-level generation is not always needed. A small set of the best task-level workflows already covers as many or more queries. That finding can cut the cost of running agent systems sharply. It tells architects to spend on a few strong workflows rather than bespoke ones for every request.
arxiv-2601-11247:
Valerie Gillot and Philippe Langevin study APN functions, a topic in finite fields. Their 2026 preprint reports new checks on the known cases. APN maps are prized in cipher design for their strength. They resist a class of attacks based on differences.

The team gives new invariants for these rare functions. They also give a test for when a function can be extended. A backtracking search then checks known facts one by one. The checks back a standing conjecture on 6-bit APN maps. The claim is that just 14 CCZ classes hold them all. Finite fields work of this kind feeds secure code and ciphers.
arxiv-2601-11347:
Sebastian Arnold and Eugenio Clerico find best e-values for a mean test. Their 2026 preprint deals with bounded random variables in statistics. An e-value is a newer tool for testing claims with data. It can grow as evidence piles up against a null claim.

The test asks if a mean beats a set rival value. The rival side is composite, a range and not a point. The team derives the unique e-values with best growth. Growth is judged in the worst case, in relative terms. The quality bar comes from work by Grunwald and others. Their frame first asked for matching hypothesis setups. This work is the first use past that strict setup.
arxiv-2601-11447:
Wadid Foudhaili and six coauthors guard secure chips with a smart monitor. Their 2026 preprint names it IMS, an intelligent monitoring system. Modern systems-on-chip talk through the AXI protocol bus. That bus has security flaws that attackers can exploit.

Protocol-violation attacks can cause denial of service on the chip. Parts or all of the chip can be forced to stall. Recent defenses lack live semantic checks of the protocol. They also evade full compliance checks in practice. IMS adds a dedicated real-time watch on AXI traffic. It checks meaning, not just form, as data flows. The aim is to catch attacks while they unfold.
arxiv-2601-11847:
Alexander Clow studies small quasi-kernels in directed graphs. A quasi-kernel is a set of nodes with no links among them. Each node in the graph must sit at most two steps from that set. Chvátal and Lovász showed in 1974 that each such graph has one.

The open part is how small such a set can be made. Clow builds them with a greedy method, step by step. Small quasi-kernels act as tight hubs for reach in a network. The work adds bounds and a clear build route for this graph problem.
arxiv-2601-12047:
Ina V. Kalitukha, Victor F. Sapega, Dmitri R. Yakovlev, and their co-authors probe spin in a lead halide perovskite crystal, CsPbBr3. They use light scattering that depends on spin, in magnetic fields up to 10 tesla. The light is tuned to exciton-polariton states in the crystal.

Their spectra show rich traits from Zeeman splits of excitons. Splits of electrons and holes that act with the excitons add more traits. Spin data guide use of such crystals in light and quantum tools. The work maps those splits with care.  Such spin maps are rare for this class of crystal.
arxiv-2601-12747:
Jingkai Li and six co authors adapt a pretrained transformer for MRI scans. These models do very well on photos of the world at large. MRI scans are a harder fit for two clear reasons. The shapes inside a body follow rules that photos do not teach. Scans are also scarce, since they are private health data.

Their model learns from scans with no labels at all, a trick called self supervision. That route needs no hand labels, which are slow and dear to make. A strong base model for MRI could lift many clinic tasks at once. Cuts, spots, and scans could all start from the same base. The work aims at a base model for health imaging as a whole.
arxiv-2601-12947:
Eslam Ibrahim, Yury Lysogorskiy, Ralf Drautz, and Pablo M. Piaggi compute the phase diagram of water from a general purpose potential. The phase diagram of water remains one of the most intricate benchmarks in molecular modeling. Many ice forms and the odd behavior of liquid water make it a stern test. Their potential is an atomic cluster expansion, a flexible machine learned model.

The potential was trained on density functional theory calculations. Those calculations use a named exchange correlation functional with dispersion corrections. Computing a full phase diagram from such a potential tests its transferability hard. A general purpose model that passes would serve many simulation tasks at once. The work matters for climate, chemistry, and materials modeling.
arxiv-2601-13147:
Jaydeb Das, Saurabh Niyogi, and Tripurari Srivastava study a lean dark matter model with a scalar gate. Their model adds two new bits to the Standard Model. One is a real scalar with no group charge. The other is a lone Dirac fermion, which plays the role of dark matter.

One twist sets their set up apart. The scalar does not take a fixed mean value at zero heat, as in the plain case. That twist links two fields of study. One is Higgs traits seen at colliders. The other is a strong first order shift in the early universe, when the electroweak force split. The paper shows how one lean model can be probed from both sides.
arxiv-2601-13347:
Aryeh Keating and Mirjeta Pasha build a step wise frame for big dynamic inverse tasks by parameter fits. An inverse task works back from data to the hidden state that made it. Big such tasks are ill posed, since the state is huge and data is thin. Rules that add past facts help, but the full form can eat more memory than any machine holds.

Their frame runs in steps. Data and state move through in a stream, so no full store is kept. At each step the model parameters are fit anew. That lets large tasks run on line as data lands. For scan and sensor teams, the frame fits tasks too big to hold at once.
arxiv-2601-13447:
Elliott P. Horch and co-authors share first three scope work with the Southern Connecticut Stellar Interferometer. The rig sits on the campus of Southern Connecticut State University in New Haven. It joins light from three scopes to read star sizes at fine scale, a task one scope cannot do.

The team gives two kinds of reads. One is a three scope read of Vega, a bright test star. That read proves the three scope mode works. They also give a fresh size read for a second star, whose name is cut in the record. For a small campus rig, three scope work that yields star sizes is a firm step.
arxiv-2601-13547:
Yujia Hu and Roy Ka-Wei Lee grade the why of hate speech flags, not just the flag. Hate speech tools are a core part of content care. Most tests score if a flag is right. Few score if the stated cause for a flag is sound. A right flag with a poor cause can still harm trust and appeals.

Their suite is called HateXScore. It holds four parts, each a mark of cause grade. Such parts can split a clear cause from a vague or off mark one. For care teams, cause grade is what a user sees on appeal. A suite to score it fills a blind spot in how such tools are judged.
arxiv-2601-13947:
Mattia Mattei, David Soriano-Paños, and Alex Arenas study how bacteria can coexist by avoiding rivalry in 2026. Bacteria regulate motility, their self-driven motion, through quorum sensing and other signals. Quorum sensing lets cells gauge how crowded their group is. Nonlinear density-dependent motility is known to create spatial patterns in active matter.

Its effect on coexistence of growing, interacting species is less explored. The team shows nonlinear competition avoidance favors coexistence in microbial populations. Species that ease off when crowded may share space in a stable way. The finding speaks to ecology and to engineered microbial groups. The result is a clear hint for work on gut and soil microbes. It may also help teams grow mixed strains in tanks with less strife.
arxiv-2601-14647:
Yuchen Fang, Xinshou Zheng, and Javad Lavaei propose an optimization method in this 2026 paper. Their method, TRSVR, is a stochastic trust-region method for unconstrained nonconvex optimization. It incorporates stochastic variance-reduced gradients, SVRG, to accelerate convergence. Classical trust-region methods limit each step to a region where the model is trusted. They usually need function value evaluations.

The proposed algorithm relies solely on stochastic gradient information. It never requires function values. Its trust-region radius is adaptively adjusted, based on a radius-control parameter and the stochastic gradient estimate. The cost is low. Each step needs just one pass of the kind used in most deep nets. The steps are few. That keeps the cost low when the task is large and the funds are tight. Readers get a step-size scheme for hard nonconvex problems where only noisy gradients are cheap.
arxiv-2601-15247:
Rian Dolphin, Joe Dursun, and co-authors pull structured risk data out of corporate filings. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with 10-K reports, the yearly filings firms must make. Each filing lists risk factors in free text, which is hard to use at scale.

The authors build a three-stage pipeline for the task. A language model first extracts risks with supporting quotes. Embedding-based mapping then ties each risk to a fixed taxonomy. A second model, acting as judge, filters out false assignments. The pipeline also improves itself on its own over time.
arxiv-2601-16647:
Baradhwaj Coleppa, Benjamin Fuks, and Akshat Khanna hunt for rare decays of the top quark. The top quark is the most heavy known basic part. In the base theory, it should not swap its flavor with no charge shift. Some wider theories say such swaps can still occur. Their 2026 preprint tests one such wider theory.

That theory adds two more Higgs fields to the known one. The three fields share a neat three-way pattern. In this frame, rare top decays arise through loops. The authors work out how large those decays could be. Their rates can then face tests at big colliders. A clear miss or hit would trim the list of live theories.
arxiv-2601-16747:
Doan-An Trieu and a team of seven co-authors push a lab route to soft X-rays. Bright bursts of high notes of light can reach that range. Such tabletop sources would aid scans of atoms and films. A weak terahertz field may stretch the burst range. Yet how that help works at weak strength was murky. Their 2026 preprint digs into that gap.

The team runs time-based quantum sims of the burst. They pair the sims with old-style path checks. A quantum path view adds a third lens on the act. The work shows how the flat top of the range grows. That growth points to brighter soft X-ray tools on a bench.
arxiv-2601-17047:
Yuanjie Gu and a team of six co-authors teach AI to read noise as a sign, not a flaw. Each scan tool leaves its own noise print on shots. That print mixes with the true scene in hard ways. Past work fought noise as mere dirt to scrub. Their 2026 preprint builds a base model that reads noise prints across shot types.

The model learns by contrast, pair by pair. It sorts prints by tool and scene traits. No vast tagged sets are needed for its train. Noise prints could flag bad gear or fake shots. They may also help join shots from unlike tools.
arxiv-2601-17147:
Margaret Garcia and a team of eight co-authors sort city water plans by how fit they stay in change. City water works now face states they weren't built for. Drought, growth, and storms push past old plans. Their 2026 preprint names dynamic fitness as the aim. That aim joins foresight with fast response in plan form. The team sorts real plans in archetypes by that aim.

Archetypes show which plan shapes bend and which break. Each shape trades foresight and response in its own way. Towns can set their plan next to the map. Weak spots then show before a crisis hits. Water boards gain a plain guide for reform.
arxiv-2601-17247:
Julius Graf and Thibaut Mastrolia study market making across a full trading day. A trading session has two parts. First comes open trade on a limit order book. Then comes a closing auction that sets the end price. Most past models treat end-of-day risk with a flat penalty on stock held. That skips the real chance the auction gives to trade.

The authors build learning into that two-part day. Their market maker can plan for the auction, not just fear it. That change should give more true quotes and risk control. For exchanges and trading firms, the work shows why the close must sit inside the model. It is where much liquidity lives.
arxiv-2601-17447:
Jorge Torres Gómez and five co-authors argue for joining literacy skills with STEM training. Well-rounded graduates need technical and soft skills at once. Most agree on that goal. Few technical schools show how to teach both in core classes. The authors build a bridge between the two schools of thought. They seek a practical path, not just a plea.

Their plan puts literacy-based skills inside the STEM curriculum. Reading, writing, and argument become part of technical work. That fit can raise the quality of reports and teamwork. It can also help engineers reach public audiences. The work serves teachers who must merge both aims in real courses.
arxiv-2601-17647:
Akila Sampath, Vandana P. Janeja, and Jianwu Wang quantify causal links in Arctic sea ice change. Ice melt and freshwater spread interact in complex ways. Their effects show as regional shifts in sea surface height. The team uses that height as a proxy for ice dynamics. They apply time-varying causal treatment methods. Those methods track effects that change over time.

Causal proof is stronger than correlation for climate choices. It can show which feedbacks drive polar change. Polar change drives global sea-level rise. Sharper causal maps help planners weigh risks to coasts. The work brings modern causal tools to a hard climate case. Time-varying effects fit a system that never stands still.
arxiv-2601-17947:
Bora Yimenicioglu and Vishal Manikanden build a label-free way to read the stiffness of red blood cells. Their 2026 preprint presents FlowMorph. Cell mechanics can flag blood and body-wide disease, so labs test how cells bend as they flow. Microfluidic tests can push thousands to millions of cells through tiny channels. Old pipelines, though, lean on hand-marked training data or hand-built charts, and they rarely use the physics of the flow itself.

FlowMorph trains itself with supervision drawn from that physics. The flow in such channels is smooth and ruled by Stokes flow laws. Using those laws as the teacher removes the need for labels. Faster, label-free tests could bring cell mechanics into wider lab use.
arxiv-2601-18047:
Amanuel Anteneh, Kyungeun Kim, J. M. Schwarz, Israel Klich, and Olivier Pfister turn laser interferometry into a learning machine. Their 2026 preprint presents an optical neural network built only from linear tools. The tools are field displacement and interferometry applied to coherent states of light. A neural network needs a nonlinear step to learn, and optics is mostly linear. The team gets the needed nonlinearity from how the input is encoded into phase.

Encoding tricks let plain optics do a smart machine's work. Light-based learning promises speed and low energy use. It may also resist some flaws of electronic hardware. The work adds a robust platform to the race for physical machine learning.
arxiv-2601-18247:
Óscar Bou Marqués and co-authors report direct views of droplets of vortex liquid in a superconductor. Their 2026 preprint studies the iron pnictide CaKFe4As4, written in the title as CaKAs4Fe4. Type-II superconductors in a magnetic field stay free of resistance while vortices stay pinned. When vortices depin, dissipation begins. Heat can melt the vortex solid into a vortex liquid, a change akin to ice melting. The team observes droplets of that liquid at half the critical temperature, in a field of 0.5 tesla.

Droplets show the melt begins in patches, not all at once. Pinning and melting set the current a superconductor can carry. Direct views guide both theory and magnet design.
arxiv-2601-18847:
Zihan Wu and four colleagues build MulVul, a team of smart agents that hunt flaws in code. A lone model is a poor fit for the hunt. Flaw kinds are too many and too un-like: what marks one kind is noise for the next. To set a lone model for each kind by hand would take a huge store of prompt craft. The team split the hunt by kind, with one agent per group of kinds.

Each agent's prompt grows by a kind of paired growth: two models trade drafts till the prompt sharpens. A search step pulls past code that fits the kind at hand, to ground each call. A wide, sharp hunt could catch flaws that a lone tool drops. It could also scale to new flaw kinds with less hand work.
arxiv-2601-19147:
Pankaj K. Agarwal and four co-authors plan the best paths for two square robots in a right angled world. The setting is a polygon with straight, axis aligned walls, possibly with holes. Each robot is a unit square that slides without turning, and both must move inside the space without clashing.

The team seeks optimal motion plans, the provably best routes for the pair. Two body planning is a classic hard case: each robot is an obstacle that moves with intent. Exact plans for even this simple case sharpen the theory behind warehouse and factory robot fleets.
arxiv-2601-19247:
Jiarun Liu and five co-authors align text, images, and 3D shapes in one shared space. Vision language models have tied words to pictures with great success. Adding the 3D sense, through point clouds and 3D Gaussians, opens training for retrieval, zero shot sorting, and scene naming across all three.

Their method, TIGaussian, disentangles the Gaussians so the alignment stays spatially aware. Knowing where things are, not just what they are, is what 3D tasks demand. Aligned text, image, and 3D data would let a user search a scene with a sentence, a fresh power for design and robotics.
arxiv-2601-19347:
Yang Ouyang and six co-authors help readers of online comments judge more fairly. Comments sway what readers think, yet their order and framing are set by platform algorithms that can bias judgment. Anchoring effects, where the first views drag later ones, are one such pull.

Their tool, CommSense, supports bias aware, reflective browsing of comment streams. It aims to slow the snap judgments that ranked comments invite. The work was shared at the CHI conference. Tools that make readers pause could lift the quality of public debate without censoring a single word.
arxiv-2601-19547:
Hiroshi Fukuda and Hiroshi Ozaki study a famous dance of three bodies in gravity. In the figure-eight choreography, three equal bodies chase each other along a single eight-shaped path. New solutions branch off from this orbit at certain points, a process called bifurcation. The authors look closely at what happens near one of these branch points.

They find cases where a branching solution folds back on itself at one side of the branch point. At the fold, the action, a key quantity in mechanics, forms a cusp. They present three worked examples under a Lennard-Jones-type force law. One more example uses a simpler homogeneous force. Such folds show how rich the three-body problem stays, even in its most famous special case.
arxiv-2601-19747:
Jiale Liu, Taiyu Zhou, and Tianqi Jiang build a framework for designing computer chips with language models. Models can now write RTL code, the register-transfer level description of a chip. Getting that code silicon-grade correct is the bottleneck. Simulation-based checks miss cases, iterative debugging can introduce regressions, and repairs can hallucinate.

Their framework, Veri-Sure, attacks all three problems. It is contract-aware, tying generation to formal statements of intent. Multiple agents share the work, and a temporal tracing system tracks changes over time. Formal verification then checks the result with proof rather than tests alone. The aim is chip designs that stay correct through the whole repair loop. The work targets a costly pain point in electronic design automation.
arxiv-2601-20047:
Divit Rawal and Sriram Vishwanath prove that curved space learns hierarchies exponentially more efficiently than flat space. Hierarchical data, like trees of categories, are common in language and biology. Euclidean embeddings of deep trees suffer volumetric collapse: too many distant leaves are squeezed close together. Hyperbolic embeddings avoid this by expanding outward.

The authors prove an exponential separation in sample complexity between the two geometries. Their setting uses hierarchies of given depth and branching under standard Lipschitz regularity. For Euclidean models, bounded radius forces the collapse; hyperbolic models escape it. The theorem gives theory to a practice already popular in representation learning. It tells practitioners when geometry choice is not a detail but the whole game.
arxiv-2601-20147:
Saima Afrin and five colleagues study how to make code summarization cheaper by choosing which tokens matter. Instruction-tuned models now write summaries of code, but feeding them whole files costs time and compute. The authors take a data-centric view: not all tokens in a code sample carry equal value for a good summary.

Their work asks which parts of the input can be trimmed while keeping summary quality high. That question matters as code models grow and usage scales up. Cutting wasted tokens would lower cost and latency for tools that document code for developers every day.
arxiv-2601-20247:
Jens Palsberg and nine colleagues report on the computer science challenges of quantum computing as it enters the era of early fault tolerance. Their report argues that progress will now be shaped as much by computer science as by better hardware. System design, integration, and evaluation become the main bottlenecks.

The authors survey what must change: compilers, programming tools, testing, and benchmarks for machines that partly correct their own errors. The report is a roadmap for researchers and funders. It makes the case that the next gains in quantum computing will come from software and systems work as much as from physics.
arxiv-2601-20347:
Chengying She and six colleagues present MMSF, a framework that joins medical images with clinical data to classify tumors and predict patient survival. Whole slide images are gigapixel scans that capture tumor shape in detail. Clinical descriptors add patient-level context for prognosis, but the two data kinds have very different statistics and scales.

MMSF is a multitask, multimodal supervised framework built on a backbone with linear complexity. It decomposes and fuses the cross-modal signals explicitly. Joining both views could give pathologists sharper risk estimates than either source alone. The hope is plain to state. Two weak views, joined well, can beat one strong view on its own.
arxiv-2601-20747:
Elham Aghakhani and Rezvaneh Rezapour study how people use AI chatbots for emotional support. Their 2026 paper draws on Reddit posts about mental health. Large language models are now often used outside clinics for comfort and advice. Yet little is known about how users judge these systems in daily life. The title phrase, like a therapist but not, captures that tension.

The team analyzed more than five thousand Reddit posts. The posts came from forty-seven mental health communities. They describe hands-on or exploratory use of AI for support or therapy. The study reads these stories to learn how people relate to the tools. It shows what users value and what worries them. Such evidence helps shape safer support tools.
arxiv-2601-21147:
Kevin Han, Haolin Cong, Bowen Deng, and Amir Farimani smooth a hidden source of error in learned atom models. Their 2026 paper concerns machine learning interatomic potentials, or MLIPs. These models power countless drug and materials discovery applications. They simulate molecular dynamics far faster than quantum methods. Two bottlenecks block realistic scales, though. Inference time is one; memory consumption is the other.

The authors target the cutoff, where atomic interactions are switched off. A sharp cutoff can jolt energies and forces. Smooth dynamic cutoffs ease that transition as atoms move. Better cutoffs mean stabler, larger simulations. The work serves anyone running MLIP-driven discovery pipelines. Small numerical kindnesses compound over millions of time steps. The paper polishes a part of the stack that many users never see.
arxiv-2601-21447:
Demetrio Lacava and Edoardo Otranto study how trade policy uncertainty moves the link between stocks and bonds. The pair uses daily United States data across a recent decade. Major stock indexes are tracked against the benchmark long-term Treasury bond.

A two-step framework based on volatility models estimates how their correlation shifts over time. Several model types, from fixed to smoothly shifting correlation, are compared. When trade news turns shaky, investors often flee stocks for bonds, which changes the link. Knowing how that link moves helps investors balance portfolios when policy risk spikes.
arxiv-2601-21647:
Eden Avrahami and Eliya Nachmani steer masked diffusion language models while they generate, without any training. These models build text by filling in blanks in parallel, a real alternative to word-by-word writing. Controls for steering them at run time are still little explored.

Their method refines the model's inner representation step by step, guided by one reference sequence. The reference pulls the output toward a desired style or content. Because nothing is retrained, the steering can be swapped per request. Run-time control matters for products that must adapt tone or obey fresh constraints on the fly.
arxiv-2601-21747:
Vincent Lemaire, Nédra Mellouli, and Pierre Jaquet model sepsis over time in a way doctors can fully read. Sepsis is among the hardest syndromes in intensive care, with varied paths and varied responses to treatment. Deep learning predicts it early but hides its reasons and ignores hidden patient subtypes.

Their relational model stays fully interpretable while tracking the patient's course. It also respects the latent groups that make one patient's sepsis unlike another's. A model a clinician can read line by line is easier to trust at the bedside. It can also teach, by showing which relations drive the risk.
arxiv-2601-21847:
Zechuan Huang and co-authors automate a piece of algorithm design that humans usually handcraft: the reward function. In meta-black-box optimization, a reinforcement learning policy learns how to design optimization algorithms. Until now, the rewards guiding that learning were written by human experts.

Human-written rewards bring design bias and invite reward hacking, where the learner games the score instead of solving the problem. The team's 2026 preprint, READY, focuses on discovering rewards automatically for this meta-optimization setting. If rewards can be learned rather than guessed, automated algorithm design changes. It becomes less dependent on expert intuition. It also becomes less prone to hidden distortions.
arxiv-2601-22447:
Yiting Liu and Zhi-Hong Deng read sparse autoencoder features by their weights, not just their firing patterns. These tools split a model's inner states into parts a human can grasp. Their 2026 preprint notes that most readings watch when a feature fires, and skip what the feature does next.

A feature exists to rebuild a state that the model then uses. Reading its outgoing weights shows that role. The shift can give truer, more useful labels for features. Better labels mean better maps of how models think. The work refines a core safety and science tool.
arxiv-2601-22547:
Shilong Zhao and a large team built PersonaAct, a set of fake short-video users that act like real ones. Platforms fear filter bubbles, where picks narrow what a user ever sees. Their 2026 preprint notes that real user studies cost much and raise privacy flags. Past simulators, built on text alone, act in thin, fake ways.

PersonaAct gives each agent a personal profile and richer behavior. Teams can then test what would happen if the platform changed its picks. Such counterfactual audits can flag bubbles before they harm. The work makes a touchy test cheap and safe.
arxiv-2601-22647:
Jinwoo Jang, Minjong Yoo, Sihyung Yoon, and Honguk Woo give embodied agents a team of world models to swap between at test time. Such agents act in the real world through language-guided plans. Their 2026 preprint notes that a fast-changing world breaks any one fixed model of it.

Their mixture keeps several world models and picks among them as the scene shifts. The idea borrows from mixture-of-experts designs. Flexible world sense should lift planning in homes, streets, and wards. The work aims at agents that adapt, not just act. It is tested in dynamic settings.
arxiv-2601-22947:
Mengyu Ye, Ryosuke Takahashi, Keito Kudo, and Jun Suzuki study a new kind of language model that fills in masked words. Masked diffusion models are a rival to the standard left-to-right approach. They match rivals on many tasks, but lag on open-ended writing.

The authors blame strict position rules: shifting a token by one place can wreck the meaning. They show this with controlled tests, then relax the alignment demand. Looser position rules could help these models write more freely while keeping their speed edge. Controlled interventions support the claim: a one-position shift alone was enough to badly damage the model's output semantics.
arxiv-2603-01547:
Sorting childhood brain tumors is hard because tissue patterns are complex and labeled cases are few. Jian Yu, Joakim Nguyen, Jinrui Fang, and colleagues combine three kinds of data to help in this 2026 study. Slide images alone miss facts held in written reports and in maps of cell nuclei.

Their system, PathMoE, joins slide images, pathology reports, and cell graphs through a set of expert models. Each expert learns what one data type adds alone, what it shares, and what emerges only when types combine. A gating step weights those experts per case, so staff can see which mix drove each call. Scores rose on both an in-house child tumor set and on outside cancer sets, with clear gains over image-only tools.
arxiv-2603-01647:
Rundong Wang, Wei Ba, Ying Zhou, and colleagues draft pathology reports from whole-slide tissue images in this 2026 work. Current tools write a broad diagnosis for a slide but fail to tie fine claims to the exact spots that support them. They also give users no way to say which details a report must hold or to check them.

Their agent, QCAgent, mimics how pathologists scan many fields of view with a goal in mind. A user checklist states the required details and limits before drafting starts. A critique step scores the draft against that list and sends the agent back to key regions. Text-to-patch search then helps revise the report so claims match visual proof. Tests show reports with more of the wanted detail and stronger clinical value.
arxiv-2603-01747:
Jan Moser revisits a lemma from a famed 1921 paper by Hardy and Littlewood in this 2026 work. That old result bounds how zeros of the Riemann zeta function spread along its critical line. The zeta function sits at the heart of deep questions about prime numbers.

Moser proves that the century-old lemma can generate a vast family of new equivalent forms. Each form restates the Fermat-Wiles theorem, the settled claim about sums of like powers, in zeta terms. The family is as large as a continuum, so the supply of such restatements has no countable end. Work of this kind links two landmark results that seem far apart on the surface. It shows how one sharp estimate can echo through very different corners of number theory.
arxiv-2603-02047:
Manuel Serna-Aguilera, Raegan Anderes, Page Daniel Dobbs, and Khoa Luu build tools to fight the nicotine public health crisis. Their 2026 work notes that flavored pouches and similar products lure young users and undo anti-tobacco gains. Past research stays narrow and cannot connect facts across very large data collections.

Their NICO data set holds over two hundred thousand multimodal samples across dozens of tobacco and nicotine brands. Images and text descriptions sit side by side for public health researchers to mine. Their retrieval system, NICO-RAG, organizes extracted entities and relations into hypergraphs at build time. Queries can then match images by look or by the semantic content of their descriptions. Tests over many questions show performance comparable to a top image-adapted rival, without costly image token processing.
arxiv-2603-02147:
Kyu Hwan Choi, Jiyong Cheon, Joonwoo Jeong, and Sho Takatori measure how molecules spread in a special liquid in this 2026 study. The liquid forms ordered stacks that guide motion in one direction more than another. They use a light method that bleaches a spot, then watches color return as molecules move in. Two dyes let them compare weak and strong ties to the stacks.

In the ordered phase, both dyes moved faster along the stack direction than across it. A dye bound tight to the stacks slowed in all directions as stacks packed closer. The loose dye sped up along the stacks, hinting at tiny channels. The results show how inner structure steers flow in soft matter.
arxiv-2603-02247:
Always-on keyword spotting must adapt on the device itself, and this 2026 paper studies how. Phones and speakers listen for a wake word under tight speed and energy limits. Voices and rooms differ, so a fixed model fits poorly over time. The three authors pair on-device training with a shrinking of the model itself.

Their method, OnDA, prunes whole channels from the network while it learns in the field. They compare pruning rules that use live user data with rules that ignore it. On two public data sets, the model shrank to about a tenth of its size at equal accuracy. On a small embedded chip, training and listening both ran faster. Energy use fell as well, which matters for always-on devices.
arxiv-2603-02347:
Yoon-Joo Kim classifies singular fibers of abelian fibrations in this 2026 mathematics paper. A fibration maps a space onto a curve, with most fibers shaped like abelian varieties. Some fibers degenerate into singular forms that need sorting. Kodaira famously sorted such fibers for the one-dimensional case, elliptic fibrations.

Kim treats minimal fibrations of any relative dimension over a curve. The work covers fibers whose main part is one dimension below the fiber itself. Three families organize the options: semistable, unstable, and multiple fibers. Multiple fibers split further into semistable-like, mixed, and unstable-like types. The result unifies Kodaira's work with later results on Lagrangian fibrations. One framework now covers all of these settings.
arxiv-2603-02447:
Satish Chandran, Nícolas Roque dos Santos, Yunshu Wu, and colleagues regularize diffusion models in the frequency domain in this 2026 paper. Diffusion models learn to turn noise into images and audio. Standard training scores each point alone, ignoring frequency and scale structure. Natural signals, though, live across many scales at once.

Their losses add Fourier and wavelet terms to the usual training objective. The diffusion process, network design, and sampling all stay unchanged. Those terms act as soft biases toward balanced frequencies and coherent fine detail. The method fits several major diffusion variants with negligible extra cost. Image and audio tests show steady quality gains. High-resolution unconditional tasks, where fine structure is hardest, gained the most.
arxiv-2603-02547:
Junzhe Shen, Jieru Zhao, Ziwei He, and Zhouhan Lin diagnose why continuous diffusion language models lag in this 2026 paper. Continuous models generate text by denoising smooth embeddings, an appealing dynamic. Discrete rivals have nonetheless performed better in practice. A controlled token-recovery study isolates where quality is lost.

The bottleneck is token rounding, the final jump from smooth vectors to discrete words. Their framework, CoDAR, keeps diffusion fully continuous in the embedding space. A strong decoder then performs the rounding, attending to the full denoised sequence. Context-aware rounding replaces the usual blind snap to the nearest token. On two text benchmarks, quality jumped over latent diffusion baselines. CoDAR became competitive with strong discrete models. A decoder temperature dial trades fluency against diversity.
arxiv-2603-02647:
Tomohiro Abe, Ryosuke Sato, and Takumu Yamanaka study a boost effect in dark matter annihilation, the process where dark matter particles destroy each other. Their 2026 paper covers the case where the products are heavier than usual and unstable, meaning they soon decay. Near the energy threshold these products move slowly.

Slow products can pull on each other over long range, which distorts their motion and can raise the annihilation rate a lot. The authors build the decay rate into the equations for the pair, rather than treating it as an afterthought. They find that bound pairs with slow decay sharpen the boost through resonance. That change shifts predictions for how much dark matter should remain today.
arxiv-2603-03247:
Brian White, Brian Blanton, Rick Luettich, and Richard Smith fuse sparse tide gauges with dense simulations to map coastal flood risk. Extreme sea level estimates from a thin gauge network carry wide uncertainty, yet physics-based simulators produce detailed output everywhere. Their 2026 two-stage framework combines both sources for the United States coast.

First, extreme value distributions are fitted at each site, allowing trends over time. Then a spatial model links the fitted parameters across sources, with correlations between interspersed gauge and simulation sites carrying information without any shared locations. Applied to four decades of records from twenty-nine gauges and one hundred simulation sites, fusion cut the error of hundred-year flood estimates by about a third versus gauges alone. Block validation confirms the gain survives extrapolation.

boole-mathematical-analysis-logic-1847:
George Boole published The Mathematical Analysis of Logic as a pamphlet in 1847. In those few pages he founded symbolic logic. Boole treated reasoning as a calculus, with symbols that could be joined and split by rule. Deduction became something like algebra, open to exact handling.

He shows how class terms and statements turn into equations. From those equations, valid conclusions follow by fixed steps. The pamphlet's claims were bold for a self taught Irish mathematician. Later thinkers built Boolean algebra on this start. That algebra now runs inside every computer on Earth. The seed text is short enough to read in one sitting.
boucher-de-perthes-antiquites-1847:
Jacques Boucher de Perthes presents flint tools in his Celtic and Antediluvian Antiquities, in French from 1847. The tools lay in gravel beds beside bones of extinct beasts. Humans, he argues, lived long before the Flood's supposed date in the old biblical reckoning of the world's age.

Learned men mocked him at first, then slowly came to see the pits themselves. His finds near Abbeville forced a new, vast age for mankind. The book gave humanity its deep past in hard stone proof. It stands as a founding document of archaeology, the work of a customs officer whose hobby rewrote human history.
boucher-de-perthes-antiquites-celtiques-:
Jacques Boucher de Perthes, a French customs man at Abbeville, brought out the first part of this work in 1847. Its title means Celtic and pre flood finds, in French. For years he had dug worked flints from deep gravel beds by the Somme.

The flints lay with the bones of beasts long dead, such as mammoths and rhinos of the ice age. Boucher de Perthes held that men made those tools in a time far past the flood of the Bible. Mocked at first, he was proved right in 1859, and a new view of man's age was born.
bronte-agnes-grey-1847:
Anne Brontë published Agnes Grey in 1847, under the name Acton Bell at first. The slim novel was her debut, a quiet account of a governess's working life in England. She drew it from her own years in service, which she had found hard and lonely.

Agnes, a parson's daughter, takes posts to help her poor family after her father's losses. Spoiled children and vain parents make her days a test of patience and self-respect in silence. She keeps her faith and her diary, and finds a friend in the curate Weston. A modest inheritance and a small school end her service on her own terms in peace. The book's plain honesty rebukes the glamor that hid governesses' real plight from readers.
bronte-jane-eyre-1847:
Charlotte Brontë published Jane Eyre in 1847, under the name Currer Bell at first. The novel became the defining first-person tale of female independence in Victorian fiction and beyond. Later governess novels and feminist coming-of-age tales all answer to its strong, plain voice here.

Jane, an orphan schooled at harsh Lowood, takes a governess post at Thornfield Hall in Yorkshire. She loves her master Rochester, whose wife, mad and hidden, lives in the attic above. Fire, a torn veil, and a voice on the wind drive the Gothic plot to crisis. Jane flees, inherits money, and returns to wed Rochester on her own free terms at last. Her insistence on equality of soul still gives the love story its sting.
bronte-wuthering-heights-1847:
Emily Brontë published Wuthering Heights in 1847, under the name Ellis Bell at first. Many call it the most radical novel of the Victorian era in form and feeling. Its storm-driven metaphysical romance broke every convention of the realist novel of its day completely.

Heathcliff, a foundling from Liverpool, is raised at Wuthering Heights on the Yorkshire moors there. His fierce bond with Catherine Earnshaw survives her marriage to Edgar Linton of the Grange. Her death drives his revenge on both houses across a whole second generation of Earnshaws. Nelly Dean and the baffled Lockwood tell the tale in frames within frames of voice. The moor wind blows through prose unlike any other English novel of its time.

The fighting stayed small in scale, but the rhetoric from Jakarta stayed loud.

The paper judges whether the raids and threats would grow, fade, or settle into a long stalemate. It weighs the cost to both sides and the growing pressure for a settlement. The study captures an odd war's late phase, when peace seemed possible yet still needed watching.
