The brigade, Cuban exiles trained by the CIA, was in its final preparation for Cuba. No subject is recorded for this item in the catalog. It survives in the original Spanish as a primary source, one more dated unit in the brigade's crowded March archive.
cia-0000136247: Dated 5 May 1954, a declassified CIA cable deals with harmless smoke grenade and flare bomb drops, ordnance for show rather than for killing. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954. Its worth is in the detail it pins down, one dated piece of a covert war fought largely on paper.
cia-0000136947: Keep the Voice of Liberty unspecific, headquarters warns LINCOLN in June 1954. Frank Wisner signed the cable. A Salvador broadcast had noted Guatemala's false claim. Guatemala said it had found and captured the station. The broadcast also cited the station's line on the Caracas declaration. That line is excellent so far. But the station must not get more specific about American programs. Its black character must be maintained. Its programs must keep an indigenous feel.
cia-0000141147:
JMWAVE, the CIA station in Miami, cabled headquarters in April 1961 to clear up the flight records of two B-26 bombers, numbers 933 and 927. Phone calls between stations had caused mix-ups, the cable says, because callers had to guard their words for security. It then sets out the corrected times: 933 left for the base called Tide, and 927 left as well.

One note ties the paperwork to a loss. The crew in question came from a B-26 that force-landed on 17 April at Boca Chica. That date was the first day of the Bay of Pigs landing, when exile-crewed bombers flew the air war over Cuba.
cia-03153747: February 22, 1958: the bulletin delivered intelligence to senior readers. The daily summary of world developments went out. The Cold War's winter briefing. Its contents inform the historical record. This file preserves that declassified paper. Kept for readers.
cia-03156047: CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1959/08/07, a CIA publication. The August briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Coming generations can find it. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Those who study the era will use it.
cia-03185147: CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1960/08/06, a CIA publication. Another August briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
cia-06626647: FOR THE SECOND TIME IN LITTLE MORE THAN A YEAR, THE ARGENTINE SUPREME COURT HA, a CIA document. The Argentine court. This file preserves that declassified paper. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
cia-06754247: USE OF BRIBES AND INTIMIDATION TACTICS BY THE NATIONALIST REPUBLICAN ALLIANCE, a CIA document. The Salvadoran tactics. This file preserves that declassified paper. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
cia-06763947: DONALD RAY WOOLBRIGHT, PLAINTIFF, V. FEDERAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION, CENTRAL, a CIA document. The lawsuit file. This file preserves that declassified paper. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
coverdale-bible-1535-bagster-1847:
Miles Coverdale gave England its first complete printed Bible in 1535, working from Latin and German versions where his Hebrew and Greek ran short. Samuel Bagster's 1847 reprint, the second modern edition, keeps the original text and spelling. The Apocrypha stands in its old place within the set.

Coverdale's phrasing of the Psalms proved so fine that the Church of England kept it in its prayer book for centuries. Lines like his rendering of the twenty-third Psalm still echo in English worship. The 1535 book was printed abroad and smuggled home at real risk. Bagster's reprint let Victorian readers hold the Tudor Bible as its first readers saw it.
davis-principles-nature-1847:
Andrew Jackson Davis speaks in trance in The Principles of Nature, his vast book of 1847. Davis was a youth from Poughkeepsie with scant school. In trance, he is said to have spoke for hours on God, stars, life, death, and the fate of man. A scribe took down each word. The book is the fruit of those long trance talks.

It came a year ere the Fox raps made his name as a seer of rank. Fans call him the John the Baptist of the new faith. The book is its first great text in his land.
demorgan-formal-logic-1847:
Augustus De Morgan, a London professor of math, published Formal Logic in 1847. Logic at the time still followed rules set by Aristotle two thousand years before. De Morgan set out to give the subject a sharper, more exact form.

He treats reasoning as a kind of calculus, where statements can be combined by clear rules. The book widens logic to cover relations and quantities, not just simple class terms. The pair of rules now called De Morgan's laws appears here in print. Later thinkers built modern symbolic logic on ground he cleared. It also picks sharp fights with the logic teaching of his day.
des-hn-bernhardi-grafen-von-der-marck-un: Des Hn. Bernhardi Grafen von der Marck und Tervis Chymische Schrifften, 1747. The count's writings. This book preserves that collection. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
doe-osti-2572823-nuclear-data-sheets-for: Nuclear Data Sheets for mass 47 got their DOE compilation, and this text covers the A=47 evaluations. The pages tabulate the levels. The nuclear data users get their reference. The sheets were A=47. The levels were tabulated. The reference was nuclear.
dumas-forty-five-guardsmen-1847:
Alexandre Dumas published The Forty-Five Guardsmen in 1847, the conclusion of his Valois trilogy in French. The romance sets Henri III's forty-five Gascon guards against the Guise faction in Paris and Anjou. Critics often call it Dumas at his most cinematic, with duels staged like film scenes.

Chicot returns, older and graver, as the king's realm frays under League and Spanish plots. The forty-five young Gascons, swaggering and loyal, guard a king who trusts almost no one near him. Diana's revenge for Bussy's murder threads through court war and the Salcede trial in Paris. Henri of Navarre waits in the wings as the Valois line nears its bloody end. The trilogy closes with the crown in peril and France on revolution's brink.
emerson-poems-1847:
Ralph Waldo Emerson published Poems in 1847, his collected verse of that early period of work. The volume holds Concord Hymn and The Rhodora, the verse counterpart to the famed essays in prose. Emerson's poems favor thought over music, yet several entered the marrow of American memory for good.

Concord Hymn, sung at the battle monument in 1837, gave us the shot heard round the world. The Rhodora finds God and beauty self-sufficing in a wild flower blooming alone in the woods. Hamatreya broods on earth owning men who thought they owned her fields and farms in Massachusetts. Brahma and Days compress his philosophy into quatrains still quoted in schools and speeches across America today. The verse shows the sage in a second, starker dress than the flowing essays.
eminent-victorians-pg2447: Strachey took four Victorian saints, Cardinal Manning, Florence Nightingale, Doctor Arnold, and General Gordon, and pricked their halos with perfect wit. The 1918 book made debunking an art. Modern biography starts here, laughing. No Victorian escaped his smile.
europmc-pmc10005347:
Dakanalis and a large team review the clinical evidence on emotional eating in a 2023 paper. Emotional eating means eating in response to feelings rather than hunger. Clinicians see it as a risk factor for gaining weight back after loss, and for harm to both body and mind.

The review gathers what studies show about links with excess weight, depression, anxiety, and daily food choices. It weighs how strong each link is and where the proof is thin. The paper helps readers sort solid findings from claims that still need better tests.
europmc-pmc10465647:
Rowson and colleagues measured head motion in football hits in 2012 to build a concussion risk curve. Concussion is a brain injury from a blow that shakes the brain. The team fixed motion sensors inside the helmets of 335 players. The gear logged each hit through games and drills.

In all, the logs held 300,977 mild hits and 57 hits that caused concussion. Rowson reports that a mild hit spun the head at 1,230 units of rotational acceleration on average. Concussion hits averaged 5,022 units, four times as hard. At 6,383 units with a matching spin speed, the risk of concussion hit 50%. The curve gives helmet makers and leagues a firm target for safer gear.
europmc-pmc10474147:
Park and co-authors traced the history of cell death research in 2023. Death was once seen as a plain end for worn-out cells, with swelling as a sure side effect. Decades of work have shown that many deaths run on gene programs. Those programs clear cells that are surplus or too damaged to keep.

Some forms are calm, such as apoptosis, the tidy self-dismantling of a cell. Others stir swelling, such as pyroptosis and necroptosis. Park lists fresh forms found in recent years, from ferroptosis to cuproptosis and erebosis. Each has its own switches and triggers. The review ties each form to health and disease, and to drug ideas that may follow.
europmc-pmc10960047:
Katsoulakis and a large team survey digital twins in health care in this 2024 review. A digital twin is a computer copy of a real thing that updates as the real thing changes. In health, such twins could model a patient, a ward, or a whole care system. Growth in big data and AI has sped this work, yet the health field is still at an early stage.

The review catalogues current uses across care management, treatment, prevention, and daily health upkeep. It examines shared research centres and notes their limits. Industry, government, and military groups all run twin projects, the authors find. The paper closes by mapping fresh research openings. The authors call for a joint global effort among all parties to turn the concept into routine care.
europmc-pmc1188247:
Dondorp and colleagues tackled a hidden problem in severe malaria in 2005. In falciparum malaria, infected red cells stick inside small vessels of vital organs. Blood counts miss those hidden parasites entirely. Yet their total load drives how sick a patient becomes.

A protein the parasite releases, called PfHRP2, offered a new measure. The team measured it in blood from 337 adults in Thailand. A model then turned protein levels into total parasite load estimates. Dondorp gives doctors a way to gauge hidden burden and judge risk. It appeared in PLoS Medicine in 2005.
europmc-pmc1193547:
Lindequist, Niedermeyer, and Jülich reviewed healing compounds in mushrooms in 2005. Mushrooms have a long record in Asian medicine. Western interest grew only in recent decades. Many species hold active compounds worth study.

Compounds covered can fight germs, viruses, and tumors in lab work. Others calm swelling, lower blood sugar, or guard the liver. Some affect the brain and immune system as well. Lindequist also touches on how such compounds get produced. The review maps a wide field for drug hunters and growers alike. Mushroom output and compound production get brief coverage too.
europmc-pmc1810547:
Solovyev and co-authors reported in 2006 how their Softberry software performed in a blind test of gene finding. The EGASP workshop asked programs to reproduce expert annotation of the human genome. Their pipeline targeted three features: genes, pseudogenes, and promoters, the start signals before genes.

The Fgenesh++ pipeline found 91 percent of coding DNA letters with 90 percent specificity on 44 test regions covering about 30 million letters. Their pseudogene finder caught 90 percent of hand-marked pseudogenes, which are dead gene copies, and found some new ones. The promoter program located 80 percent of one promoter class with one false hit per 2,000 letters. For the harder class without that signal, it found half, with one false hit per 650 letters.
europmc-pmc1904447:
Rosa, Vieta and co-authors validated in 2007 a short test of daily functioning for people with bipolar disorder. Many patients struggle at work, in relationships, and in self-care even when mood symptoms remit. Most existing tools give one global score instead of showing which life domains fail.

Their test, named FAST, has 24 items across six areas: autonomy, work, thinking, finances, relationships, and leisure. They gave it to 101 patients in a Barcelona bipolar program and 61 healthy controls. Internal consistency came out very high in the results reported. The study also checked agreement with other measures. It tested whether scores separate patients in an acute episode from those in remission. Factor structure and the stability of repeat scores were also examined. The aim was a brief, domain-level tool for clinic and research.
europmc-pmc2072847:
Apelberg and colleagues studied in 2007 whether two fluorinated chemicals in newborn cord blood relate to birth size. Animal studies had shown developmental harm from PFOS and PFOA. The team analysed cord serum from 293 single births in Baltimore, Maryland. Cord blood reflects exposure in the womb. Mothers' details and babies' measurements came from medical charts.

After adjusting for other factors, both chemicals linked to lower birth weight and smaller head size. Each rise in PFOS corresponded to about 69 grams lower weight, and each rise in PFOA to about 104 grams lower, though the intervals included zero. A body proportion measure, the ponderal index, fell significantly for both. Neither chemical linked to newborn length or pregnancy duration. The authors urge replication in other populations.
europmc-pmc2124647: A medical paper studying the cause of increased portal pressure. The liver's veins. This article preserves that experimental research. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2125147: How polio ravaged the body was mapped in this pathology paper on epidemic poliomyelitis. The virus's trail through tissue. The article preserves that pathological study. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Preserved for study.
europmc-pmc2125547: A medical paper with studies on the metabolism of cells in vitro, toxicity of amino acids. The cultured cells' food. This article preserves that cell biology. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2125947: A medical paper studying the antiseptic properties of certain organic compounds. The germ killers. This article preserves that pharmacology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2128147: A medical paper with experimental studies on inflammation and chemicals' influence. The inflamed tissue. This article preserves that pathology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2128247: Another medical paper on experimental rabbit syphilis, primary scrotal infection. The rabbit pox again. This article preserves that venereology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
europmc-pmc2128347: A medical paper on blood destruction during exercise, exercise as bone marrow stimulus. The athlete's blood. This article preserves that physiology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2128447: A medical paper on the lung volume in heart disease. The cardiac lungs. This article preserves that cardiology. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2131247: A medical paper on local specific therapy of experimental pneumococcal meningitis, experiments. The brain cure again. This article preserves that therapeutics. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2140447: A biology paper on the production of volatile fatty acids by bacteria of the dysentery group. The smelly acids. This article preserves that bacteriology. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it.
europmc-pmc2220047:
Hämäläinen and co-workers screened 36 plant flavonoids in 2007 for anti-inflammatory effects in macrophages. These immune cells, when triggered by bacterial products, make large amounts of nitric oxide via an enzyme called iNOS. Blocking that output is a marker of anti-inflammatory action. The team exposed macrophages to a bacterial stimulus and measured nitric oxide, iNOS levels and two transcription factors that switch iNOS on.

Eight compounds blocked iNOS and nitric oxide production in a dose-dependent way. They included flavone, genistein, quercetin and naringenin. All eight inhibited activation of NF-kappaB, one switch for iNOS. Four of them, genistein, kaempferol, quercetin and daidzein, also blocked the second switch, STAT-1. The others inhibited only NF-kappaB. The split mechanisms partly explain how dietary flavonoids calm inflammation.
europmc-pmc2243147:
van Vliet, Heijenbrok-Kal, Hunink, Kuipers and Siersema pooled studies in 2008 comparing three scans for staging oesophageal cancer. Staging tells whether cancer has spread, guiding curative or palliative choices. The methods were endoscopic ultrasound, computed tomography and FDG-PET, a metabolic scan. The team searched PubMed for studies before January 2006 reporting full test accuracy data for lymph node and distant spread, then pooled sensitivity and specificity statistically.

For regional lymph nodes, endoscopic ultrasound was the most sensitive method at 0.80, while CT and PET were more specific, so they proved better at ruling spread in when a result came back positive. This pooled analysis covered the published staging studies. For distant metastases, PET beat CT clearly on sensitivity, at 0.71 against 0.52, and it was also the more specific of the two. The authors suggest each test plays a distinctive role in staging.
europmc-pmc2361347:
Weisberg and co-authors reviewed AMN107, later named nilotinib, a new drug for leukaemia. The target diseases, chronic myelogenous leukaemia and one form of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, are driven by a faulty gene called BCR-ABL. The standard drug imatinib blocks that gene's protein, but many advanced patients relapse when the gene mutates.

AMN107 was designed to grip the protein's binding pocket more tightly than imatinib. It proved stronger against the normal protein, working at doses under 30 nanomolar, and it stayed active against 32 of 33 imatinib-resistant mutants tested. In lab and animal studies it attacked both normal and resistant cells. Early patient trials then produced blood and chromosome responses in people who had failed imatinib or never responded to it.
europmc-pmc2430947:
Eisenmann reviewed a continuous risk score for metabolic syndrome in children in 2008. Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of problems: belly fat, high blood pressure, high blood sugar and fats, and low protective cholesterol. With childhood obesity rising, the syndrome now appears in youth, but no agreed definition exists for them.

Estimates put the condition in about 2% to 10% of young people, depending on the cut-offs used. Because yes-or-no labels miss borderline children and rates are low, researchers built a continuous score instead. The score adds up each child's graded risk factors into one composite index. Eisenmann explains how such scores are derived from the underlying measurements and standardised against reference groups. He argues the score tracks risk more sensitively in population studies, and suits tracking change over time better than a fixed diagnosis.
europmc-pmc2528947:
Wirth and colleagues reconstructed the deep history of the tuberculosis bacteria in this 2008 study. This group, the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, is among the most successful human pathogens, yet when and where it arose was disputed. The team used repeating DNA sequences as genetic markers across many strains from humans and animals.

Their tree split into two branches: one holding only human tuberculosis lineages, and one mixing animal and human strains, itself likely descended from a human lineage. That pattern supports an original human host rather than a jump from cattle. Dating the tree put the group's age near 40,000 years, matching the modern human expansion out of Africa. Most lineages then swelled recently, in step with the human population explosion of the last two centuries.
europmc-pmc2667647:
Gibson and co-authors found in 2009 that the antibody-making cell mix of some very old people collapses into a narrow set of clones. B cells produce antibodies, and variety in their ranks is what lets the body meet new germs. The team read B-cell patterns in blood from people aged 86 to 94, and compared them with adults under 55.

A share of the elders showed a dramatic loss of variety. Reading the DNA showed the cause: a few B-cell families had multiplied hugely, crowding out the rest. The loss tracked health closely. People with narrowed ranks were more often frail, and the pattern linked with shorter survival and low vitamin B12 levels as well. A blood test of this kind, the authors say, could flag immune frailty and general frailty together.
europmc-pmc2684747:
Hahne and co-authors released in 2009 flowCore, a software package for handling flow cytometry data at modern scale. Flow cytometry reads single cells as they stream past lasers, a workhorse method in immunology and drug trials. Automation had swollen experiments to thousands of samples, but analysis tools still assumed small, hand-run studies.

Built for the R language inside the Bioconductor project, flowCore gives researchers shared data structures that hold whole cohorts at once. The same steps can then run across every sample in a study, instead of one file at a time. That shared frame lets statisticians, programmers, and clinicians build on each other's work rather than start over. Several later packages already stand on it. The authors argue that common plumbing, unglamorous as it sounds, is what lets a field model rich trial data properly.
europmc-pmc2744247:
Howard and co-authors studied in 2009 azole resistance in Aspergillus fumigatus. This mold causes severe lung and invasive disease in people with weak immunity. They also tracked how resistance evolves during treatment failure. Azoles are the only licensed oral drug class for this disease, so cross-resistance would remove that option. Resistance usually comes from changes in the drug target gene, cyp51A.

Screening a large referral laboratory collection gathered from 1992 to 2007, they found resistant isolates linked to patients whose treatment had failed. Resistant strains carried cyp51A mutations at known hotspots and often resisted several azoles at once. Typing showed distinct strains rather than one outbreak clone, which suggests resistance emerges within patients under drug pressure.
europmc-pmc2753847:
Nielsen and Lund presented NN-align in 2009. The neural network method predicts which peptides bind MHC class II molecules. Those molecules show fragments from outside the cell to helper T cells. Predicting binding helps explain host-pathogen interactions and guides vaccine work. Class II binding is harder than class I because peptides vary more in length and binding core position.

NN-align finds the binding core and the binding affinity at the same time, and corrects bias from redundant cores in training data. Adding information about residues flanking the core significantly improved accuracy. On a large benchmark of six data sets covering fourteen human class II variants, it outperformed other state-of-the-art methods and was released as a public web service.
europmc-pmc2760147:
Selmecki, Dulmage, Cowen, Anderson, and Berman tracked in 2009 how extra chromosomes evolve during drug resistance in Candida albicans, a common human fungal pathogen. Resistance to fluconazole, the most used drug for it, is often linked to aneuploidy, an abnormal chromosome count. Its dynamics over time were unclear. They ran a controlled lab evolution study with and without the drug.

No extra chromosomes appeared in drug-free populations. In every drug-treated population, an extra chromosome arm appeared soon after exposure. It raised fitness in the drug and became fixed over time. Further gains coincided with the highest resistance levels. Some carriers were fitter even without the drug, which helps explain why resistance persists in patients.
europmc-pmc2763347:
Urban and co-authors showed in 2009 that neutrophil extracellular traps carry calprotectin. The traps are web-like structures neutrophils release to catch microbes. Calprotectin is their main antifungal weapon against Candida albicans. The traps were known to ensnare and kill microbes, but their full protein makeup and killing mechanism were unclear. The team mapped trap proteins with proteomics and high-resolution electron microscopy.

They identified twenty-four trap-associated proteins, largely modified nucleosomes plus a strict selection of others, several of them from the cell's interior. Calprotectin, a two-protein complex, proved to be the major antifungal part: traps lacking it lost all antifungal activity in the dish. In three mouse infection models, calprotectin was crucial for clearing the fungus, confirming its role in living hosts. Careful counting of the trap contents made that case hard to dispute.
europmc-pmc2770847:
Fredholm and co-authors asked in 2009 why breast cancer in young women carries a worse outlook despite intensive treatment. Breast cancer is uncommon under forty yet still the most frequent cancer in that group. Using a registry cohort of over twenty-two thousand women diagnosed from 1992 to 2005, they compared survival across age bands and stages.

Five-year relative survival was lowest in women aged twenty to thirty-four. Their excess death risk, nearly triple that of women in their fifties and sixties, appeared only in stages I and II. It peaked in tiny tumors of one centimeter or less, where it rose almost sevenfold. The youngest women generally got more aggressive treatment than older patients. After adjusting for stage, tumor traits, and treatment, age under thirty-five stayed an independent risk factor for death.
europmc-pmc2788247:
Joppa and Pfaff showed in 2009 that the world's protected areas sit in biased locations, high and far from the land conversion they are meant to stop. About an eighth of Earth's land is protected, most of it during the twentieth century. They tested the networks of one hundred forty-seven nations for bias in elevation, slope, distance to roads and cities, and farm suitability.

The significant majority of national networks leaned toward higher elevations and steeper slopes. They also sat farther from roads and cities than chance would give. Within countries, the most strictly protected areas were the most biased of all. Protection, in short, clusters where conversion pressure is weakest, even if every reserve worked perfectly. Siting rules applied country by country, and carbon payments that reward avoided deforestation, could redirect protection toward threatened land.
europmc-pmc2829047:
Wooley, Godzik, and Friedberg wrote a primer in 2010 on metagenomics, the study of whole microbial communities through their DNA without growing them in a lab. Cheaper, faster sequencing now lets researchers sample microbes straight from soil, sea, or gut. A sample can hold over ten thousand species, and its sequence data arrive noisy and in fragments.

The primer walks through each computing step, from sampling and piecing fragments together to spotting genes and guessing their jobs. It notes which software tools exist for each step and how well they serve. Sample studies close the piece, showing finds the approach has already produced. The authors stress that sorting signal from millions of mixed sequences remains the field's core challenge.
europmc-pmc2872647:
Heinrich and co-authors showed in 2010 that support cells from the brain's cortex can be converted into working nerve cells of chosen types. The support cells, called astroglia, share a birthplace with neurons but normally never fire signals. Forcing single master genes for early brain development into cultured astroglia had turned some into neurons before, yet the kinds made were poorly controlled.

By picking the master gene to match a target, the team steered cells toward either excitatory neurons, which pass signals on, or inhibitory ones, which damp signals down. The converted cells formed synapses, the contact points neurons use to talk, and fired in the patterns of their chosen kind. Stable conversion of local support cells hints at a repair route that uses the brain's own spare cells.
europmc-pmc2901947:
Meyer and the IberoAmerican Cryptococcal Study Group typed in 2003 three hundred forty isolates of Cryptococcus neoformans. The yeast causes life-threatening lung and brain infection. The isolates came from nine Latin American countries and Spain. Two DNA fingerprint methods sorted the isolates into the eight known molecular types, building the region's first baseline map of this pathogen.

One type, VNI, accounted for over two thirds of all isolates, matching its global dominance in human disease. The remaining types appeared in smaller shares, including four types belonging to the sibling species variety that carries different surface markers. A few hybrid isolates showed a gene pattern never reported before. Regional typing lets future outbreaks be matched against this baseline to trace sources.
europmc-pmc2916847:
Saccone and a vast consortium meta-analyzed in 2010 the chromosome 15 region that genetics had tied to smoking, lung cancer, and lung disease. The region holds the genes for nicotine receptor parts, and one variant had been linked to how much people smoke. With extensive genotyping across many cohorts, the team asked whether one signal or several independent ones drive the associations.

They resolved multiple independent loci in the region, each affecting smoking quantity on its own. The famous receptor variant was joined by at least two statistically separate signals tagged by other markers. Patterns for lung cancer and chronic lung disease lined up with the smoking effects, consistent with genes acting through cigarette consumption rather than directly on the lung. Untangling the loci matters for judging whether the region also harms the lung outright.
europmc-pmc3053347:
Bouyer and colleagues showed in 2011 that a gene silencing system controls the moment a plant seedling must stop living like an embryo. The system, called PRC2 in short, places a repressive mark on DNA packaging proteins and keeps whole gene sets off. By working around its role in seed food tissue, the team grew plants fully lacking one of its core parts.

Without the system, the repressive mark vanished across the genome, yet the basic body plan still formed normally. Seeds instead stayed dormant too long and germinated poorly, as if stuck in the embryo phase. Seedlings that did sprout soon stalled and grew tumor like lumps instead of proper shoots. Only some target genes switched on, and master control genes were among them. The authors call the system a robust guard of life phase changes in plants.
europmc-pmc3056147:
Nuytemans, Theuns, Cruts, and Van Broeckhoven updated in 2010 the catalog of inherited changes behind familial Parkinson disease. Five genes are firmly tied to the disease, and more than five hundred distinct changes in them had been reported. Most are simple letter changes in the gene code, while roughly a fifth are missing or extra copies of whole sections.

The team organized every published change into a free online database so doctors and researchers can check a new finding against all known ones. They warn that some change types are likely undercounted, because few studies checked all five genes for both kinds of change. The same genes also turn up in related brain conditions with similar protein clumps. The authors urge full screening of patients, followed by lab work to prove which changes truly cause disease.
europmc-pmc3084247:
Hörnberg and colleagues reported in 2011 that shortened versions of the androgen receptor in prostate cancer that has spread to bone mark the most stubborn and deadly cases. Normal prostate growth is driven by male hormones acting on this receptor. Cancers that keep growing after hormone blocking treatment sometimes make receptor variants that lack the hormone sensing end and stay permanently on.

The team measured these variants in bone metastases, the most important spread site, comparing cancers never treated with hormone blockade against resistant ones. Variant levels were clearly higher in resistant tumors, and one variant appeared only there. Tumors with the highest variant levels, about a third of resistant cases, showed disturbed cell cycle control and the patients died sooner. The authors propose testing whether such patients gain more from drugs that attack the receptor's working end directly.
europmc-pmc3164647:
Rebecca Corrigan and colleagues discovered a new signalling molecule in a major hospital pathogen in a 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. The bacterium's wall polymer is vital for growth, yet rare mutants survive without it. Sequencing those survivors revealed changes in one gene, pointing to a cyclic molecule the gene's enzyme destroys.

The team showed the molecule is genuinely made in this species by a dedicated builder enzyme, and that blocking its destruction sends its levels soaring. High levels thickened the wall's cross-linking, perhaps compensating for the missing polymer, and shrank cell size noticeably. The messenger thus helps control cell size and helps the bacterium endure wall stress, a fresh angle on a pathogen famous for drug resistance.
europmc-pmc3179347:
Ulrike Mödder and colleagues measured a bone-formation brake in the blood of nearly seven hundred adults in a 2011 paper in the Journal of Bone and Mineral Research. The protein, made by bone-embedded cells, blocks a key growth signal. Nothing was known about how its blood level varies with age, sex, or bone mass in people, so the team sampled a whole community age range.

Men carried clearly higher levels than women. Levels climbed steeply across life, more than doubling in women and rising several-fold in men. At any given amount of bone, older people carried more of the brake than younger people. The age rise may help explain why bone formation falters late in life, and the study gives the reference patterns needed before the protein can serve as a clinical marker.
europmc-pmc3179447:
Shlomo Rotshenker reviewed how injured peripheral nerves clear the way for their own regrowth in a 2011 paper in the Journal of Neuroinflammation. When a nerve is cut or crushed, the segment beyond the injury must be remodelled before new fibres can grow through it to their targets. That remodelling, a process named over a century ago, is run largely by the innate immune system.

Support cells, fibroblasts, scavenger immune cells, and vessel cells act in concert, stripping away growth-blocking insulation debris and switching on nourishing properties. europmc-pmc3186747:
Philipp Schuetz, Werner Albrich, and Beat Mueller reviewed a blood marker that guides antibiotic use in a 2011 paper in BMC Medicine. Standard infection tests are slow or vague, so antibiotics are often started blindly and run too long, breeding resistance. The marker, procalcitonin, rises far more specifically in bacterial infection, and trials had tested algorithms built on it.

For chest infections, post-surgery infections, and severe sepsis in intensive care, randomised trials showed marker-guided decisions safely cut antibiotic starts and durations. For other infections, early observational results look promising but trials are still needed. The review weighs the marker's reliability inside validated algorithms and charts where evidence is firm, where it is thin, and what studies come next.
europmc-pmc3206047:
Tuomas Kilpeläinen, Ruth Loos, and a very large group of collaborators pooled data from many studies in this 2011 meta-analysis of the FTO gene and obesity. FTO variants raise the risk of obesity, and the team asked whether being physically active softens that genetic effect. Their combined sample covered more than two hundred thousand adults and about nineteen thousand children.

Across the adult studies, physical activity substantially weakened the link between the FTO risk variant and obesity. In other words, the gene's effect was not fixed: active adults carrying the risk version fared noticeably better than inactive carriers. The work supports a gene-and-lifestyle view of obesity, where daily activity can partly offset an inherited tendency to gain weight.
europmc-pmc3257747:
Krista Crider, Lynn Bailey, and Robert Berry reviewed folic acid food fortification in this 2011 article in Nutrients. Taking folic acid around conception is known to cut a woman's risk of a baby with a neural tube defect, a serious malformation of the brain or spine. Many countries therefore require folic acid to be added to staple foods, and defect rates have fallen worldwide.

At the same time, worries persist about unintended consequences of higher population-wide intake. The authors trace the history of fortification programs, measure their effects, and air the concerns. Their message is that uncertainty makes continued monitoring essential, so programs can prove their benefits with accurate measures and respond as questions arise. The review ends by looking at where fortification policy may go next.
europmc-pmc3291347:
Wang and co-authors reviewed what was known about bats and the SARS virus in 2006. SARS had swept through many countries in 2002 and 2003 before being stopped, and its cause was a coronavirus new to science. The authors gathered evidence on where the virus came from and whether similar viruses still circulate in animals.

Work in animal markets found viruses nearly identical to the human one, and traders showed higher rates of past infection than other people. Most striking, researchers had found a varied set of SARS like coronaviruses living in horseshoe bats. The review argues that bats are a likely source pool, so fresh outbreaks from animal viruses remain a real risk.
europmc-pmc3298247:
Kilpatrick and colleagues built a better way to judge which mosquitoes spread West Nile virus to people, in a 2005 study. Control programs in the northeastern United States lacked clear targets because the roles of different species were poorly known. Their measure combined how many mosquitoes of each kind are present, how often they carry the virus, how well they pass it on, and how often they bite people.

Two Culex species that officials had largely overlooked came out on top. Together they may account for most human infections in the region, up to roughly four fifths. Focusing control on those two species could cut human cases while sparing wetland wildlife, and the authors say the same scoring method can be adapted to other places and diseases.
europmc-pmc3323247:
Morris and a large group of colleagues reviewed the changing pattern of a lung infection that preys on weakened immune systems, in a 2004 article. The infection, called PCP, is caused by a fungus like organism and was once the illness that first revealed AIDS in most patients. Strong HIV drug combinations had cut its numbers sharply by the time of the review.

Even so, PCP remained the most common serious opportunistic illness in people with HIV, especially where treatment is unavailable. The authors describe who stays at risk in rich and poor countries alike, including transplant patients and others on immune suppressing drugs. A growing worry is whether the organism is mutating toward resistance against the standard preventive antibiotic. The article introduces a series on that question and urges standardized data collection.
europmc-pmc3340347:
Monasta and colleagues produced the first global estimates of the burden of middle ear disease, in a 2012 review. Middle ear infections, called otitis media, are a leading reason children see doctors and receive antibiotics. Their complications are a major cause of preventable hearing loss, especially in poorer countries, yet no worldwide tally existed within the global burden of disease project.

Drawing on more than one hundred studies, the team estimated hundreds of millions of acute ear infections each year. Over half of them strike children under five. The chronic draining form adds tens of millions of cases, and roughly twenty one thousand people die yearly from complications such as meningitis. Hearing loss tied to the disease affects tens of millions. The authors urge ear focused action inside child health programs.
europmc-pmc3399847:
Krakauer and Krakauer proposed a new body measure in 2012, arguing that the standard body mass index misses the risk carried in body shape. Waist size hints at belly fat, but it rises and falls with body mass index itself, so its extra signal is hard to isolate. Their index, called ABSI, adjusts waist size for height and weight directly.

Built from a national survey of more than fourteen thousand American adults followed for about five years, the index barely correlated with height, weight, or body mass index. Death rates climbed steadily as it rose above average, and the link survived adjustment for smoking, diabetes, blood pressure, and cholesterol. Shape, they conclude, forecasts early death in its own right.

fbi-roswell-teletype-1947:
Dallas wired Washington the first federal word on Roswell on the night of July 8, 1947. The teletype from Percy Wyly, the FBI chief in Dallas, sends on the Eighth Air Force report of a found disc. The wire went out at 6:17 in the evening, as the tale broke.

Wyly tells that Wright Field has not yet backed the weather balloon line the Army would soon give out. The disc, by the wire, was on its way east for study. The brisk lines catch the case at its first hour, before the cover tale set. The teletype is the Roswell story's first paper trail.
frus-1861-d147:
William Dayton sent a second dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 August 1861. It is document 147 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

A second report in one day points to more than one live thread in Paris. Dayton split his points as Seward split his orders. The letter adds depth to a crowded week in the French file of 1861. Threads in Paris ranged from cotton prices to the fate of ships in French yards. Each thread he held was thin alone and strong only in the whole weave.
frus-1861-d247:
Orders from Washington reached James Shepherd Pike in a State Department letter dated 15 August 1861. It stands as Document 247 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. It belongs to the first summer of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d47:
Charles Francis Adams sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 21 May 1861, the same day Seward wrote to him. It is document 47 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The two men wrote past each other across the ocean, each unaware of the other's page. Adams reported his first dealings in London while Seward drafted stern orders at home. The matched date shows how wide the gap was between the post and the capital. The British proclamation of neutrality came that same week, which raised the stakes of each page.
frus-1862-d147:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to London on 19 September 1862, addressing Charles Francis Adams, the American minister there. The dispatch survives as Document 147 in the 1862 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's printed record of its dealings abroad.

Two days earlier the armies had met at Antietam, and President Lincoln was about to act on slavery. Word of both moves would reach Europe slowly and could shift how London saw the war. A short official letter like this one was the tool Washington had for guiding its envoy through fast-moving weeks. Adams held the London post from 1861 to 1868, the longest run of any Union envoy in Europe.
frus-1862-d247:
A second Seward dispatch to Paris followed on 28 December 1861, printed as Document 247 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to William L. Dayton, the American minister to France, from Secretary of State William H. Seward.

Two letters in three days mark the New Year rush of business after the Trent settlement. Dayton needed fresh guidance for a French government that was landing troops in Mexico that very month, alongside Britain and Spain. The pairing of these dispatches shows Washington trying to steady two fronts at once as 1862 began. French mills wanted Southern cotton, and French yards watched the Union blockade with care.
frus-1862-d347:
The Paris file in this run closes with a Seward dispatch to William L. Dayton dated 21 November 1862, printed as Document 347 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton was the American minister to France.

Late November found the joint-action danger past for the year and France turning its energy back to Mexico. Seward's letter of this date belongs to the winding down of the autumn crisis in the Paris channel. It ends the Dayton sequence on the steadier ground the Union had sought since spring. French public opinion ran warmer for the Union after the emancipation news arrived. Dayton, a former senator from New Jersey, held the Paris post from 1861 until his death in 1864.
frus-1862-d447:
Hermann Kreismann, the American consul in Berlin, wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 August 1862. It is Document 447 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Consular letters rarely made headlines, but they carried the facts of everyday foreign business: trade, shipping, stranded seamen, and citizens in trouble. Kreismann wrote from a capital friendly to the Union in a month when Union arms were stalled in Virginia. A consul's report also passed along the talk of the streets and papers, which ministers sometimes missed. The letter adds a ground-level Prussian view to the volume's record of the war's second summer.
frus-1862-d47:
Orders from Washington reached Charles Francis Adams in a State Department letter dated 14 April 1862. It stands as Document 47 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The letter comes from the spring of 1862, a year into the war, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d547:
Roest van Limburg wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 29 September 1862. His note is Document 547 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, with the heading punctuated as printed in the volume.

Van Limburg wrote a week after Lincoln's preliminary emancipation order, which changed the moral weather of every diplomatic conversation in Washington. The Dutch, strongly antislavery at home, received that change with interest. The formal business of the note belonged to the usual file of trade and neutral right, but it was transacted in a new atmosphere. The letter belongs to the early autumn Dutch papers. In them the reader can sense the war becoming a different kind of war. In European eyes, it was no longer the war of the spring.
frus-1862-d647:
Writing on 5 May 1862, Robert H. Pruyn sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. Pruyn had just taken charge of the American legation in Japan, a post set up only in the late 1850s. The letter stands as document 647 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

In these first weeks Pruyn wrote home about the legation's work and his dealings with Japan's rulers. Such reports were how Washington learned what its envoys saw, weeks after the fact, since mail moved by ship. The dispatch is one link in the chain that kept a young trade link alive during a war an ocean away.
frus-1863p1-d147:
Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 8 April 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 147 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

April mail from London followed up the seizure of the Southern raider and weighed what would come next in the yards. Adams kept his reports plain and full, as Seward liked them. This dispatch is a mid-run piece of that follow-up. It shows the legation turning a win into a watch: one ship held did not end the South's hopes in Britain, and Adams knew it.
frus-1863p1-d247:
Writing from London on 24 July 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. The dispatch is document 247 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

In 1863 the great question in London was whether Britain would treat the Confederacy as a real nation. Adams's reports helped Washington judge that risk week by week. It was written in the month of Gettysburg and Vicksburg, twin Union wins that changed how Europe judged the war. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d347:
The American answer to London on 31 December 1862 took the form of this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 347 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

The two men met and wrote constantly, and both knew a quarrel between their countries could hand the South its independence. That shared fear kept the tone correct even when the words were sharp. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d447:
On 4 April 1863, William H. Seward, the Secretary of State wrote to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d47:
Christopher G. Memminger wrote this letter to James M. Mason on 24 October 1862. Memminger was the Confederate secretary of the treasury; Mason was the South's envoy in London. The letter is document 47 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The treasury's letters to London dealt with the South's thin purse: loans, cotton, and the bills that piled up in Europe. Memminger wrote to the man who faced the bankers and the British press. This letter is one of the money papers in the Confederate group printed here. It shows the war's other front, fought with credit in the counting houses of London.
frus-1863p1-d547:
On 1 June 1863 a formal note passed from Assistant Secretary of State F. W. Seward to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d647:
On 24 October 1863, William H. Seward, Secretary of State wrote to the American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams. Mail between London and Washington crossed the Atlantic by steamer, so each reply took weeks to complete the round trip. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863.

Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. That autumn the sharpest issue was the pair of ironclad rams built for the Confederacy at Birkenhead. Britain held them back, and this mail ran while that fight played out. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d147: A second letter from Roosevelt to Ambassador Steinhardt is dated November 20, 1943, and it stands as Document 147 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. With the secretary's letter of the same date, the day's Turkish traffic in this volume runs to three items, the heaviest for any embassy that month. The record does not divide their errands. All are printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d247:
Minutes of the Joint Chiefs of Staff meeting at Cairo on 22 November 1943, at eleven in the morning, record a session called mainly to hear the theater envoys. General Marshall opened by inviting Ambassador Winant, back from London, to describe British thinking, with Ambassador Harriman and theater representatives also present.

Winant says the British felt Allied gains in Italy were not being used fast enough, and saw chances to act and to draw Turkey into the war. On Overlord, he reports no wish to drop the operation, but strong resistance to a fixed date, since London feared a signed contract that ignored later changes. The British also wanted Balkan resistance fully used, and in Italy aimed at Rome and its airfields, not the Po valley.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d347:
Harry Hopkins sent Ambassador Kirk detailed release instructions for the Cairo communiqué from Tehran on 29 November 1943. The short telegram, approved by President Roosevelt, fixes one of the tightest press timetables of the conference.

Kirk is to give the text to the Office of War Information for publication at half past eleven at night, Greenwich time, on Wednesday 1 December, under a Cairo dateline. News services get the text at five on Tuesday afternoon in Cairo to allow transmission. They get it under strict warning. All of it stays secret until the release hour, with no advance statements or speculation of any kind. Stories must note that all the principals have left Cairo for unannounced destinations, and pictures are released at the same hour. Kirk must also notify the Chinese minister in detail and send the full instructions and text at highest priority to Steve Early in Washington.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d447:
Yet another Combined Chiefs of Staff session fell on December 5, 1943, and its minutes appear in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume. The chiefs, the senior American and British officers who ran the combined war effort, were meeting daily at the Second Cairo Conference. Their task was to settle the strategy that Tehran had only sketched.

The minutes lay out the session in order: attendance, the matters raised, and the decisions the chiefs recorded before passing them to Roosevelt and Churchill. Together with the day's other records, this one helps show a conference working at full speed. It is primary evidence of how the alliance made its hardest military choices.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d47: On October 19, 1943, the day the Moscow Conference opened, Stalin wrote to Roosevelt again. His message is Document 47 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The timing gives the letter its setting even though the record gives it no topic: ministers were meeting in Moscow while the heads of government kept writing over their heads. The message survives in the Foreign Relations series, in the heart of the October papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d547:
Ambassador John Gilbert Winant sent a second direct report to President Roosevelt from London on January 14, 1944. Winant's access in Britain, where he was almost a national figure, made his presidential channel unusually rich. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

Two Winant reports to the President inside a fortnight show London business pressing on Washington that January. Britain was then straining under six years of war while preparing to host the invasion of France. For readers, Winant's direct reports offer the feel of the allied capital from a man both governments trusted, written while the Tehran and Cairo decisions were being put into practice.
frus-1944-quebec-d147:
Writing from Hyde Park on September 3, 1944, Roosevelt answered Churchill's latest Italian telegram, number 774. He shared the prime minister's confidence that the Allied divisions in Italy were sufficient for the task before them. Their commanders, he trusted, would press the battle unrelentingly to shatter the enemy forces on the Gothic Line.

After that breakthrough, Roosevelt insisted, the divisions must be used where they best aided Eisenhower's decisive drive into Germany. He leaned toward using American forces westward but called himself completely open-minded. The exact employment could be discussed at Octagon. He closed by crediting General Wilson and General Patch impartially for the brilliant success in southern France.
frus-1944-quebec-d247: Hopkins telegraphed Grace Tully, the president's secretary, on September 15, 1944, chasing a decision. He had sent Roosevelt the State Department's September 11 memorandum on the French lend-lease agreement. The Foreign Economic Administration and the State Department were anxious to know whether the president had initialed it. Hopkins asked Tully to help him get an answer the next day.
frus-1944-quebec-d47:
Roosevelt wrote again to Churchill on September 1, 1944. It was the second presidential message of the day. The State Department printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume.

By September 1944, the two men had corresponded for five years of war. Their habits were set by then. Separate papers covered separate questions, and answers came in kind. Roosevelt's twin messages close the day's work between the capitals. For readers, the pair shows how the allies governed together. They governed at a distance and in writing. Meanwhile, armies moved faster than any conference could follow.
frus-1945-50-intel-d147:
The title "Central Intelligence Group Administrative Order No. 3" heads a text dated 19 April 1946. It is document 147 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The postwar system was still new: the National Intelligence Authority gave the orders, and the Central Intelligence Group carried them out.

Papers of this kind were the working stock of the system. They were drafted, read, marked up, and filed so the next office could pick up the thread. Read with its neighbors, it helps fill the gaps that grand accounts skip over. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d247:
The Deputy Director (Wright) addressed a memorandum to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter on 4 November 1947. Readers meet it as document 247 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The shift from the old group to the CIA was fresh. The Council was still learning how to run its side of the work.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d347:
The Executive Secretary of the Intelligence Survey Group (Blum) addressed a memorandum to the Intelligence Advisory Committee on 10 June 1948. The State Department prints it as document 347 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. By then the National Security Council met often, and questions about secret operations abroad were moving to the center of its work.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d47:
A memorandum of a meeting held on 19 November 1945 follows the staff committee papers in the volume. It records a session rather than a single author's view. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Memoranda of meetings catch the points where plans met resistance or merged. In November 1945 those meetings came thick and fast, since the president's men wanted an intelligence plan ready for the new year. Readers tracking the endgame of the autumn fight should slow down here. The run of November papers shows the rival drafts being trimmed toward a compromise. That compromise became the National Intelligence Authority in January 1946.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d147:
Mikolajczyk explained his resignation to an American diplomat in London, and the report reached Washington on 25 November 1944. Ambassador Winant's cable passes on Schoenfeld's account of their talk that morning. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

He resigned, Mikolajczyk said, because he held a settlement with Moscow to be a necessity now. The three other main parties in his coalition wanted the frontier question left until the war ended. Without a settlement, he reasoned, Poland faced the loss of its eastern lands with no sure gain in the west. Worse, the country would face hard drives toward communism, with the Lublin Committee already largely Communist in make-up. A quick return by London Poles might still stop that.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d247:
Korea's future handling should be settled among the allies in advance, this briefing book paper argues. “Inter-Allied Consultation Regarding Korea,” dated 13 January 1945, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It poses two questions for agreement with Britain and China, and perhaps with Russia.

Who should share in the military occupation of Korea? And who should sit in an interim world administration or trusteeship, if one is set up? The Department holds that Korea's problems are of such world concern that the occupation force should carry allied representation. The seats should go to states with a real interest in Korea's future. Those are the United States, Britain, China, and the Soviet Union if she has entered the Pacific war. Care is added that American strength in the force not be thinned.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d347:
H. Freeman Matthews jotted these rough notes at the foreign ministers' lunch table at Yalta on February 6, 1945. Copied from his pencil longhand, they track the same talks Page recorded in full minutes. Stettinius backed a first communiqué. Molotov liked it and wanted "common" added before "enemy." There was no bar to naming the Black Sea area.

Then came surrender terms. All three agreed to add "dismemberment" to Article 12, after the word for demilitarization. Eden tried a softer formula about ending the German unitary state. No deal was reached on the Russian change. The shorthand scraps let readers watch a clause being born.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d447:
A Balkan federation is the ghost behind this British paper of February 10, 1945. London had already told Moscow its views on a possible Yugoslav-Bulgarian federation. In reply, the Soviet government reported knowing that Yugoslav and Bulgarian talks on a pact of alliance were proceeding. Moscow's attitude toward such a pact was favorable.

At the same time, Moscow judged a Balkan federation not a live question of practical importance just then. Britain, the paper says, was glad to learn that view. The careful courtesies hide a real fear: that Tito's Yugoslavia and Bulgaria might merge under Soviet blessing, shifting the Balkan balance.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d47: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on 8 January 1945, the same day Harriman reported from Moscow. The letter is document 47 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences, published by the Department of State. Placed side by side, the two messages show the president hearing from his British partner and his Soviet ambassador within a single day.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d147:
Harry Hopkins sent a second report from Moscow on May 30, 1945, on Stalin's plans for the peace. The extract is document 147 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Hopkins had pressed Stalin on several questions that would face the three leaders at their coming meeting.

Stalin twice stressed planning at once for a formal peace conference on Europe, warning that the Allies had gone to Versailles unprepared and must not repeat the mistake. On Germany, Hopkins corrected Stalin's belief that London and Washington opposed dismemberment; the question stayed open, and Stalin said he would keep an open mind. Hopkins also expects Stalin to bring specific proposals on prisoners of war and, above all, war criminals.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d247:
A briefing paper recommended trusteeship for the Somali colonies in a paper dated June 30, 1945. The paper is document 247 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It covers Italian Somaliland, on the Horn of Africa, one of the colonies Italy stood to lose in the peace settlement.

Italian Somaliland, together with the French and British Somali territories, should go under international trusteeship, the paper holds. A workable alternative would put the Italian and British territories under trusteeship while leaving French Somaliland French, with a genuinely free port at Jibuti. The data section notes a colony of 194,000 square miles and about a million people, almost all Somalis. It was begun in the 1880s. It was folded into Italian East Africa after the conquest of Ethiopia. Its value lay in its position on the Indian Ocean near the Red Sea entrance.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d347:
Denazification is again the theme of Murphy's despatch No. 576 from Frankfurt, dated July 7, 1945, this time in extracts. General Clay, Murphy reports, had thought of holding a press conference on the purge of Nazis. Clay asked the Political Division to prepare the basic facts such a conference would need.

An informal interdivisional committee on denazification then weighed whether the conference was wise, and what form it should take. The extracts print the basic questions and the fundamental points drawn up for Clay's use. They show the occupation shaping not just a purge, but the public story it would tell Germans about that purge.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d447:
MacVeagh, the ambassador in Athens, welcomed Washington's attention to Greek election supervision in his cable of July 9, 1945. The fundamental local situation, he warns, is unchanged, and his comments rest on his reporting since December 1944. Russian participation, he believes, is essential: it would satisfy the Left and allay suspicions, and so pacify the country.

He asks what form supervision would take. Friendly observers, present to influence events and later pass on the vote's fairness, are one thing. Actual intervention at the polls, with British troops supervising, is another. That, he argues, might let Moscow charge a violation of Greek sovereignty and stir endless argument over undue influence. The British chargé, Caccia, agreed.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d47:
Prime Minister Churchill protested to President Truman on June 1, 1945, that the planned Big Three meeting was set too late. His personal and top secret telegram is document 47 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Churchill had gladly agreed to come to Berlin, but not on Truman's chosen date of July 15.

July 15, he writes, is much too late for the urgent questions that demand attention, and delay would injure world hopes and unity. Even in the middle of a hard-fought election at home, he would put the meeting first. He presses for June 15 instead, or failing that July 1, 2, or 3. He also tells Truman he has sent a copy of the message to Stalin.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d547:
State Department staff wrote a top secret briefing paper on civil aviation and Great Britain for the Potsdam Conference. Dated June 21, 1945, it is document 547 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers. It was meant to arm President Truman for talks with the British prime minister.

The paper lists four points to raise. Britain, it says, works to block U.S. air lines in Europe and the Near and Middle East. Britain also blocks sales of U.S. planes in sterling areas. The U.S. is ready to sign a two-way air pact, and the peace treaties should cover flying rights too. It backs the five freedoms agreed at Chicago in December 1944, of which Britain had taken only two.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d647:
Loy Henderson, director of Near Eastern and African Affairs, recorded a meeting with Zionist leaders on June 28, 1945. His memo is document 647 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Acting Secretary Grew received the group in Washington that afternoon.

The visitors were Rabbi Stephen Wise, Nahum Goldmann, Chaim Greenberg, and a Mr. Shulman. Grew said he had read with care a memo Goldmann had given Henderson days before. It set out the problems the Zionists faced and their views on Palestine's future. Grew noted a growing demand among U.S. Zionists for decisive steps on Palestine in the near future. The memo preserves the start of a lobbying push that would run through the Potsdam weeks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1047:
Edwin Pauley laid out Germany's food balance for the Secretary of State in this letter of July 28, 1945. His staff worked from official statistics. In 1936, Germany within its 1937 borders lacked 5.7 million tons of food overall. The zone now held by the USSR ran a surplus of 2.65 million tons. The western zones thus faced a shortfall of 8.35 million tons.

Pauley projects the coming years. Farm collections will drop, city diets will shrink, and grain imports must fill the gap. Germany as a whole will need some 4.4 million tons of grain a year. He also arms Byrnes with a talking point for Molotov: western equipment sent east is a free gift, while eastern food would be paid for in Reichsmarks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1147:
George Kennan in Moscow wrote to Matwin, the Polish envoy there, on 23 July 1945. Kennan was the senior American diplomat in the Soviet capital at the time. His note crossed the lines of the alliance: an American writing to a Pole, inside Moscow, while Poland's fate was debated in Germany.

Embassy-level contact of this kind kept working ties alive between posts. The two men dealt with the daily business their embassies shared in the same capital. The note is a small human thread inside great-power bargaining. It shows that even as leaders argued over Poland, their envoys still had to talk to each other.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1247:
Hurley addressed this message to the President and the Secretary of State on 25 July 1945. Writing to both men at once marked the dispatch for the highest level. Hurley's China reports kept the summit's leaders tied to the Asian half of the war.

China's crisis ran on its own clock, indifferent to the German talks. A government weakening, armies watching each other, and Japan's defeat nearing made Hurley's file urgent in its own right. This message carried his word to the top at Potsdam. It is one of the threads that kept the China war inside the summit's field of view.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1347:
Secretary of State James Byrnes wrote to Lowell Pinkerton, the American consul general at Jerusalem, on 18 August 1945. The letter came two weeks after the Potsdam Conference closed. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Jerusalem was one of the most charged posts in the American service in 1945, with the future of Palestine drawing pressure from many sides. A letter from the secretary of state himself shows the question reaching the highest level of the department. It also shows the Potsdam volume reaching past the summit's end date to follow the business the conference left behind.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-147: This brief editorial note, printed without a number after document 710, comes from the Potsdam volume's editors. In the Foreign Relations series, editors' notes stand apart from the wartime texts. They supply orientation: dates, sources, and links the documents omit. The note serves readers who want to follow the paper trail with care.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-47:
A United States delegation memorandum of July 20, 1945, holds notes on a Soviet suggestion to internationalize the Ruhr. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The exchange took place in the economic subcommittee, with Maisky speaking for the Soviet side.

Maisky proposed placing the Ruhr, an area of four million people, under the four powers jointly. The body would regulate the Ruhr's production to ensure control of the German war potential. Pressed on details, he said the whole industrial area was meant, as soon as possible, and more or less permanently. A special organization, not the Control Council, would likely run it. The Western men held back in reply. Monckton and Clayton both called the scheme political as well as economic, beyond their committee's instructions. Pauley's figures put the district at twenty-five by fifty miles of coal and industry.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d747:
Cannon wrote from Lisbon to Assistant Secretary James Dunn on July 19, 1945, in document 747. The first secretary at the Lisbon embassy reported up the Department's ladder. Portugal's neutral ground made it a crossroads of rumor and quiet contact. Cannon's letter joined the second Potsdam volume.

A report to an assistant secretary travels fast. Dunn stood close to the Secretary and could act on what he read. Readers see information climbing from a listening post to the center. The document shows the Department's reach during the conference: while the leaders met, its ears stayed open in every capital that mattered.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d847:
Emilio Collado and a colleague named Rubin wrote jointly on August 2, 1945, in document 847. Collado directed the office of financial and development policy. Their letter went to an acting division chief as the Potsdam Conference closed that day. The paper joined the second Potsdam volume.

A closing-day staff letter on money matters shows the peace being costed. Financial officers had to turn summit lines into workable plans. Readers see that translation beginning at once. The document adds the Treasury-minded view to the volume's end. Potsdam's promises would live or die in offices like Collado's, and this letter shows the handoff starting.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d947:
William Clayton put his reparations views on record for the Secretary of State in this memorandum of July 29, 1945. He says it confirms what he told the Secretary that morning. Clayton concedes that talk at Yalta and Moscow gave Russia reason to expect half of all reparations in kind from Germany.

Only a zonal split can work in practice, he argues. The Russian zone holds 40 percent of movable factory equipment, mostly light industry. The west holds the heavy gear Russia wants, half of it in the Ruhr. Clayton proposes a trade: Russian and Polish claims met from their zone plus a quarter of Ruhr removals. A like amount more would swap for eastern food, coal, and timber.
frus-1958-60v10p1-d147: A 1958-1960 FRUS document from the Eastern Europe and Soviet Union volume. The bloc watched. This entry preserves that record. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
gao-gaoreports-b-295547: McKinley Construction & Excavating broke ground on a March 2005 protest, and GAO's ruling is the decision. The builders' claims were measured against the award. The foundation of the verdict was the merits. The merits held firm. The decision was solid. The ground was firm.
gao-gaoreports-b-296847: Chapman Law Firm took its September 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298247: Fabritech doubled its July 2006 protest — two case numbers, one tech fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer each, and the record stays clean.
gao-gaoreports-b-299547: Northwest Heritage Consultants took its May 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. The firm said the agency's award was unfair; the call tests the protest against bid law. Heritage consulting deals get the same fair-play hearing as any federal buy.
gao-gaoreports-b-309947: A 2007 GAO ruling on a contract fight from Central Texas College. The school said the agency's training-deal award was unfair; the ruling tests the claim and gives the final say. The call shows GAO's bid court serving classrooms as well as corporations — fair play rules apply to campus bidders too.
gao-gaoreports-b-311247: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Lisa Hartman-Designated Employee Agent. The May 6, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The full text sits with this description in the library.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-547: Athens Olympics security got a GAO review in 2005, and the report says U.S. support offered lessons for future games. The findings gather the wisdom. The report shows the games' guard was studied. The lessons had to be learned. The games' guard was studied.
