Their subject was CCR5Δ32 genotypes in a german HIV-1 seroconverter cohort and report of HIV-1 infection in a CCR5Δ32 homozygous individual. Authorship is credited in the record to Djin-Ye Oh and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Homozygosity (Δ32/Δ32) for the 32 bp deletion in the chemokine receptor 5 (CCR5) gene is associated with strong resistance against HIV infection. It goes on to note a further point. Heterozygosity is associated with protection of HIV-1 disease progression. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002847:
Haixi Miao and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was gene expression and functional studies of the optic nerve head astrocyte transcriptome from normal african americans and caucasian americans donors. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Haixi Miao, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. To determine whether optic nerve head (ONH) astrocytes, a key cellular component of glaucomatous neuropathy. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002947:
Nancy Cladel, Jiafen Hu, Karla Balogh and co-authors recoded a papillomavirus gene in 2008 to see what changed. Papillomaviruses use rare codons, the three-letter DNA words for amino acids, compared with their hosts. Matching viral codons to host ones can raise protein output, past studies had shown.

The team optimized codons in the CRPV E7 gene without changing the protein itself. Growth and immunity shifted, including after E7 vaccination. Published in PLOS ONE, the result warns vaccine designers that silent DNA changes are not always silent in the body. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003047:
Sandra Taylor and Katherine Pollard compared two methods for estimating bird populations in 2008. Effective management depends on tracking how bird numbers trend over time, and sometimes on estimating total abundance. Two methods had been advocated for such studies: double observer and double sampling.

Published in PLOS ONE, the evaluation sets the two against each other so field crews can choose with evidence. Double observer uses paired counters; double sampling pairs quick counts with intensive ones. Getting trends right matters because management money follows the numbers these methods produce. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003147:
Sera L. Young, M. Jeffrey Wilson, Dennis Miller and colleagues tackle a methods gap on pica in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Pica is the craving for and eating of non-food items such as earth, charcoal and raw starch. It has puzzled people for more than two thousand years, yet few data exist to test the main ideas about it, in part due to weak methods.

The authors propose a full approach to collecting and analysing pica substances, with a focus on earth-eating materials. Readers get practical steps for field and lab work on a neglected behaviour. Better samples should let future studies test why pica occurs and whether it harms or helps.
plos-pone-0003247:
Genc Basha, Gregory Lizée, Anna T. Reinicke and colleagues trace antigen handling in dendritic cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Cross-presentation by dendritic cells is a crucial prerequisite for effective priming of cytotoxic T-cell responses against bacterial, viral and tumour antigens. However, this antigen presentation pathway remains poorly defined. The team set out to develop a comprehensive understanding of it.

They report that MHC class I endosomal and lysosomal trafficking coincides with exogenous antigen loading in dendritic cells. Readers follow the route foreign material takes to reach the display system. That route is a target for improving vaccines that need strong T-cell responses.
plos-pone-0003347:
Hilda Fragoso-Loyo and co-authors test antibody measures in lupus that affects the brain in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Lupus, or systemic lupus erythematosus, can involve the brain and nerves, but that diagnosis is hard and unsure. Past work tried to link some serum antibodies to those brain symptoms. The team assess those antibodies in blood and spinal fluid.

Readers get a check on which autoantibodies track with neuropsychiatric lupus, and what that means for diagnosis and cause. Brain lupus has few firm tests, so even a partial marker can aid doctors who must act on weak signs.
plos-pone-0003447:
Victoria Kolupaeva, Emmanuel Laplantine, and Claudio Basilico traced a stop signal for cartilage cells in 2008. A growth factor called FGF tells these cells to halt division. That halt depends on two proteins from the Rb family, p107 and p130. The team asked how p107 gets switched into its active state.

An enzyme called PP2A removes a phosphate tag from p107. That removal proved critical for the cell cycle arrest FGF causes. Faulty FGF receptors cause several genetic skeletal disorders. Pinpointing this step names a place where the faulty signal might be softened.
plos-pone-0003547:
Robert Brudevold, Torstein Hole, and Jens Hammerstrøm studied high ferritin levels in patients in this 2008 paper. Referrals for hyperferritinemia had risen over ten years. Awareness of an iron overload disease and its gene test drove many referrals. Yet most referred patients had no iron overload at all.

In those patients, high ferritin linked to insulin resistance and fatty liver. Ferritin stores iron, but here it flagged metabolic trouble instead. The work reframes a common lab result as a warning sign. It may spare patients needless iron-focused testing. Fatty liver is rising fast with obesity in most rich countries.
plos-pone-0003647:
Carola Engler, Romy Kandzia, and Sylvestre Marillonnet published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. Cloning means joining DNA pieces in a set order to build new constructs. Older methods often leave extra sequence scars in the final product. The team set out to remove that flaw.

Their method joins pieces in one pot and one step, with precise joins and no leftover recombination sites. It also works at high throughput, so many constructs can be built at once. For labs, it offers a cleaner and faster route to assembled genes than the tools it replaced.
plos-pone-0003747:
Anan Yaghmur, Peter Laggner, Mats Almgren, and colleagues published this materials study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Monoelaidin is a fat-like compound that assembles itself in water into tiny structures. With a polymer stabilizer present, those structures change with temperature. The team watched the changes closely.

Using X-ray scattering and cryo-electron microscopy, they proved a direct shift from simple vesicles to cubosomes. Cubosomes are particles with a complex inner grid. Mapping this self-assembly guides designs for drug delivery particles built from such shape-shifting fats. Heat alone drove the change, with no new parts added.
plos-pone-0003847:
Gianni Panagiotou, Mikael R. Andersen, Thomas Grotkjær, and colleagues published this systems biology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Aspergillus nidulans is a model fungus, close kin to species used in industry. The team identified the gene for a metabolic route in it called the phosphoketolase pathway.

Through systems analysis they unfolded how that pathway relates to the fungus's growth. The route reroutes sugar breakdown, and its activity sets part of the mold's pace of life. The work shows how a metabolic shortcut can shape growth in a model eukaryote used across cell biology.
plos-pone-0003947:
Klaus M. Stiefel, Boris S. Gutkin, and Terrence J. Sejnowski modeled how a brain chemical resets neuron timing in 2008. Cortical neurons fire spikes shaped by many inner currents. A phase response curve shows how a nudge shifts the next spike's timing. Neuromodulators can reshape that curve in living tissue.

Their PLOS ONE article studies acetylcholine, a classic modulator in the cortex. They report it changes both the shape and type of the response curve. That change alters how pyramid-shaped cortical neurons sync with inputs. The result helps explain how attention chemicals retune brain circuits.
plos-pone-0004047:
Jungnam Lee, Kyudong Han, Thomas J. Meyer, and co-authors traced flips in human and chimp chromosomes in 2008. Mobile DNA elements make up much of the human genome. LINE-1 elements form about 21 percent and Alu about 11 percent. Since humans and chimps diverged, those elements kept reshaping chromosomes.

Their PLOS ONE article blames retrotransposons for many chromosomal inversions. An inversion reverses a DNA segment's direction along the chromosome. Such flips can separate populations and shape evolution. The work shows jumping genes as major architects of genome structure. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004147:
Qiu-Hong Wan and colleagues published this genome study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The giant panda's major histocompatibility complex, or MHC, is a set of genes that helps the immune system tell self from invader. The team set out to learn the structure and history of these genes in the panda.

They read a stretch of DNA over 636,000 letters long covering the MHC class II region. Their analysis traces how these genes were born and lost over time, a pattern called the birth-and-death process. The map gives conservation scientists a genetic tool for a rare species and a case study in how immune genes evolve.
plos-pone-0004247:
Junji Sagara, Toshiaki Arata, and Shunichiro Taniguchi published this cell study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Scapinin, also called phactr3, is a protein that binds both actin, the cell's scaffolding fibre, and protein phosphatase 1. It is made in the adult brain and in some tumour cells, but its roles were poorly understood.

The authors show that a repeat region of scapinin grabs the actin cytoskeleton. They report that scapinin enhances cell spreading and motility by interacting with that skeleton. A protein that helps cells spread and move matters in both brain wiring and tumour spread.
plos-pone-0004347:
Isabelle Desguerre and colleagues published this muscular dystrophy study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Duchenne muscular dystrophy varies greatly between patients, and that clinical heterogeneity is a major obstacle to interpreting therapeutic trials. To explore it, the team carried out a retrospective, single-institution, long-term follow-up study of patients with complete lack of muscle dystrophin. All lacked dystrophin, the protein whose absence defines the disease.

From those records they define sub-phenotypes, distinct patterns within the disease, and predictive criteria for how it will unfold. Sorting patients into meaningful groups makes future trials fairer and their results readable.
plos-pone-0004447:
Very slow waves roll through the brain's thalamus, and Magor Lorincz, Freya Geall, Ying Bao, and co-authors linked them to the cell fuel ATP in PLOS ONE in 2009. Brain scans in people and animals show spontaneous slow swings in activity, slower than one cycle in ten seconds. These infra-slow oscillations seem to be a basic feature of how the brain works.

The thalamus is a relay station deep in the brain. Working with thalamic networks, the team showed the slow waves depend on ATP, the molecule cells burn for energy. That tie between energy supply and brain rhythm is notable. It suggests the brain's background hum is not free, and may falter when energy runs short, as in some brain disorders.
plos-pone-0004547:
Protein production can now be watched inside single chosen cell types of a living animal, show Nikos Kourtis and Nektarios Tavernarakis in PLOS ONE in 2009. Measuring protein synthesis, general and specific, gives key information about how cells work. The standard method feeds cells radioactive amino acids and tracks them into new proteins.

That method cannot be applied in a cell-specific way inside a whole organism: every cell takes up the label. The authors present a method for cell-specific monitoring of protein synthesis in vivo. Picking out one cell type in a living body lets researchers ask how, say, nerve cells alone respond to disease or drugs. The tool opens a level of detail that bulk measurements blur away.
plos-pone-0004647:
A member of the RAF kinase family works in the cell's recycling traffic, show Elena Nekhoroshkova, Stefan Albert, Matthias Becker, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. RAF kinases direct the ERK MAPK signaling pathway to distinct compartments inside cells in response to growth factor stimulation. Of the three mammalian forms, A-RAF is special: one of its fat-binding domains gives it a unique pattern of membrane localization.

The team shows A-RAF functions in endocytic membrane traffic regulated by ARF6, a switch protein of the internal transport system. Endocytosis pulls material from the cell surface into internal sacs for sorting and reuse. Tying a famous cancer-related kinase to that traffic system expands its known jobs, and may matter for how growth signals are timed.
plos-pone-0004747:
Kelvin Wong and colleagues set out and tested a way to track fluid motion from MRI scans, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their method uses radio signal patterns in scan pixels of a moving fluid. From those patterns it can build two way maps of flow direction and speed across the scan.

The team lays out the theory and checks it against known flows. Good flow maps from standard scans could help doctors judge heart and vessel health. They could also aid engineers who study fluid motion in soft, living tissue. No extra tracer or surgery is needed.
plos-pone-0004847:
Brandon Kuczenski led a team that built a tool to probe how cells react to changing doses for PLOS ONE in 2009. Cells in the body rarely face one fixed dose of a signal. Doses rise and fall in waves, and cells read those waves as they grow, move, and respond to drugs or to stress.

The tool, a tiny fluid device, can apply smooth dose waves at set spots. Cells can thus be watched as dose goes up and down in a set rhythm. How cells react to rhythm, not just to dose size, can now be tested with care. That should help drug tests match real life in the body more closely.
plos-pone-0004947:
Syndecan-1 is a protein that sits across the cell surface. It wears long sugar chains. It also turns up inside the cell nucleus, where its role is unclear. Ligong Chen and Ralph Sanderson studied what controls it there. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They focused on heparanase, an enzyme that trims those sugar chains.

Heparanase was known to change syndecan-1 at the surface. The team showed it also sets syndecan-1 levels in the nucleus. That links surface events to the cell's command center. The finding opens new questions. What does nuclear syndecan-1 actually do once it gets there?
plos-pone-0005047:
The brain constantly predicts what comes next. Reading is a perfect test of that prediction. Michael Dambacher and colleagues recorded brain waves during reading. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They used event-related potentials. The recordings differ between predicted words and unexpected ones.

Predicted visual input gets verified remarkably fast. Expectation-based and input-driven streams converge within milliseconds. The study catches the brain's fact-checker in action. It shows reading is not passive intake. The mind guesses, then checks the guess against the eyes. That check shapes comprehension speed. The work maps how prediction and sight meet during an everyday act.
plos-pone-0005147:
Group A Streptococcus causes strep throat and worse. No vaccine against it exists yet. Manisha Pandey, Michael Batzloff and Michael Good studied a leading candidate in PLOS ONE in 2009. The candidate is called J8-DT. It protects mice against the germ. The question was how that protection works.

Both B cells and T cells contribute to the protection. J8-specific antibodies lead the defense after vaccination. The study broke the immune mechanism into its parts. Knowing the recipe guides the push toward a human vaccine. Strep infections can trigger rheumatic heart disease. A working vaccine would prevent that damage worldwide. This mechanism study is a step on that road.
plos-pone-0005247:
Hepatitis D virus is a defective virus that cannot spread without hepatitis B virus to carry it. Infection with D happens only alongside B, or on top of an existing B infection. Xiridou and colleagues modeled control of the pair in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Because the two viruses are bound together, programs aimed at B alone may fall short. The modeling shows how D can hinder efforts to control B. Planners who ignore the hitchhiker risk overestimating what vaccination and treatment for B can achieve on their own. The lesson is plain: a plan that treats one virus and ignores the other may look good on paper and still fail in the field.
plos-pone-0005347:
When DNA strands swap during recombination, they form a cross-shaped structure called a Holliday junction. An enzyme named RuvC must cut that junction twice to finish the swap in E. coli. Osman and colleagues worked out what the second cut requires in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Efficient second strand cleavage needed two things at once: a more flexible junction and an exposed phosphate at the five-prime end. Those requirements show how the enzyme stages its cuts in order. Precise cutting matters, since sloppy resolution would scramble the genome it is meant to repair.
plos-pone-0005447:
Devinder Kaur and co-authors studied unusual sugars made by mycobacteria in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. These bacteria make two families of complex sugars inside their cells. No one fully knows what jobs those sugars do for the germ.

The team traced the first steps by which one sugar family is built. They pinned down the enzymes and starting parts involved in getting the process going. Knowing how the sugars are made is a first step toward learning why the germ needs them. Blocking them might weaken bacteria that cause tuberculosis and related diseases.
plos-pone-0005547:
Xiangguo Qiu and co-authors tested an Ebola vaccine in monkeys for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The Zaire form of Ebola virus causes a lethal fever with bleeding in people and monkeys. A vaccine that works by mouth or nose would be easier to give in an outbreak than one by injection.

The team gave monkeys a vaccine built on a harmless carrier virus, by nose, mouth, or injection, a month before exposure. All routes raised strong responses against Ebola and protected the animals. Flexible delivery could speed vaccination when an outbreak strikes.
plos-pone-0005647:
Marit van Vonderen and co-authors studied fat loss during HIV treatment in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Loss of limb fat is a known side effect of some HIV drugs, most clearly one called stavudine. Whether a widely used drug pair also causes it was less certain.

The team followed patients on a zidovudine and lamivudine pair and measured limb fat over time. They found that the pair does contribute to fat loss, though less sharply than stavudine. Patients and doctors need that knowledge when choosing long-term HIV regimens. Fat loss of this kind can be mistaken for disease progress, which makes its drug cause worth naming clearly.
plos-pone-0005747:
Caroline Benn and co-authors tested in 2009 whether lowering one gene's activity eases Huntington's disease in mice. Huntington's is a fatal inherited brain disease with no treatment that slows it. Faulty gene control inside cells is part of the damage, so enzymes that tune genes are drug targets.

The team reduced HDAC7, one such tuning enzyme, in the R6/2 mouse model. The disease course did not improve. A clear negative result still guides the field: effort can shift to other HDAC types. The study shows why each candidate must be tested alone, not assumed to help as a class.
plos-pone-0005847:
Julio Pérez-Andino, Christopher Buck, and Katharina Ribbeck showed in 2009 that human papillomavirus can stick to live human sperm. HPVs infect skin and mucosal tissue, and the high-risk types cause nearly all cervical cancer. They spread through sexual contact, but the fine route was not fully pinned down.

The team demonstrated HPV16 adsorbing onto sperm cells directly. Sperm could thus carry virus to a partner's tissues, a route worth probing. The finding may matter for fertility clinics and for understanding transmission beyond skin contact. It adds a concrete step to a transmission story often left vague.
plos-pone-0005947:
Glioblastoma, a fast-growing brain tumor, often holds patches starved of oxygen. Anastasia Murat, Eugenia Migliavacca, Farzana Hussain and colleagues asked in 2009 how that low oxygen rewires the tumor. Their PLOS ONE paper uses gene activity profiles to track two responses: growth of new blood vessels and inflammation inside the tumor.

Low oxygen is easy to spot in these tumors, since dead patches and dense vessels are signs doctors use to name the disease. The gene profiles show how the tumor answers that stress in ways that may help it spread. Learning which genes switch on could point to drug targets that cut off the tumor's response to its own harsh setting.
plos-pone-0006047:
Blood-sucking insects drink a meal that could destroy their own gut. Veruska Barros, Jéssica Assumpção, André Cadete and colleagues studied the gut's shield in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper covers triatomine bugs and mosquitoes, whose saliva and gut carry inhibitors of the complement system, a blood weapon that marks invaders for destruction.

The obvious job of those inhibitors is to guard the midgut while it holds fresh blood. Knowing the shield's parts helps explain how these insects feed safely. It may also expose weak points in insects that carry disease, since a gut left unguarded against complement could make blood feeding a far riskier meal.
plos-pone-0006147:
Two proteins tied to inflammatory disease change each other's place in the cell. Andrea Waite, Philip Schaner, Neil Richards and colleagues studied that interplay in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper covers PSTPIP1, an adaptor that links phosphatases to their targets, and pyrin, its binding partner. Mutations in PSTPIP1 cause PAPA syndrome, an autoinflammatory disease of joints and skin with severe acne.

Pyrin modulates where PSTPIP1 sits inside the cell, the title reports. A changed address can change which targets the adaptor serves, which may be how the disease mutations do their harm. The work gives PAPA research a mechanism to test, in a rare disease whose lessons reach common inflammation.
plos-pone-0006247:
Memory may be written in the exact timing of nerve impulses, not just in which cells fire. Jian Liu and Zhen-Su She built a neural network model based on spike-timing patterns in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Evidence is growing that precisely timed spiking carries real information in the brain.

Their model treats memory states as patterns spread over time. It lets researchers test how such patterns form, persist, and are recalled. Models of this kind bridge brain recordings and theory. They also guide designs for artificial networks that use timing, an approach most software networks ignore.
plos-pone-0006347:
Females of many species mate with several males and often raise better offspring for it. Laura McLeod and Dustin Marshall tested one explanation in a marine invertebrate in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Multiple mating may raise genetic diversity among offspring, or it may favour compatible males and sperm competition.

Their test asks whether diversity effects themselves drive the benefits of polyandry. Separating diversity from mate quality is tricky but essential. The answer shapes how biologists read mating behaviour across animals. Even simple marine creatures can arbitrate big evolutionary debates. The study shows how much care is needed before broad claims can be made.
plos-pone-0006447:
Thomas Kelder and co-authors opened a data service for biologists in PLOS ONE in 2009. WikiPathways is a shared platform where scientists create, update, and share maps of biological pathways. People could already edit and download pathways through its wiki-style website. The team added a way for software to reach the same data directly.

They present a SOAP web service that gives programmatic access to WikiPathways. Programs can now search and pull pathway data without a human clicking through pages. That makes large-scale mining of pathway knowledge practical. The service complements the website and widens who, and what, can use the resource.
plos-pone-0006547:
Xiaolin Shi, Lada Adamic, Belle Tseng, and colleagues measured boundary-spanning work in science and patents for PLOS ONE in 2009. Human knowledge and innovation are recorded in two media: scholarly publications and patents. These records document new scientific insights and new methods alike. The authors study work that spans boundaries between fields or between science and technology.

They assess the impact of such boundary-spanning publications and patents. Work that bridges areas may be cited more, or may struggle to find an audience. The answer matters for universities and funders that promote interdisciplinary research. The study uses large publication and patent databases.
plos-pone-0006647:
Julie Jodoin, Micheal Misiewicz, Priya Makhijani, and colleagues studied prion protein mutants and cell death in PLOS ONE in 2009. Previously, they had shown loss of anti-Bax function in prion protein mutants associated with Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Those mutants cannot generate cytosolic prion protein properly. The team extended the work to Gerstmann-Sträussler-Scheinker syndrome-associated prion mutants.

Their title reports loss of anti-Bax function in those mutants too. Healthy prion protein restrains Bax, a driver of cell death; disease mutants lose that protection. A shared mechanism across prion diseases is valuable. It suggests protecting neurons from Bax could help broadly.
plos-pone-0006747:
Ron Pinhasi and Noreen von Cramon-Taubadel used skull measurements to test how farming spread into Europe in PLOS ONE in 2009. The debate is old and crosses several fields. Geneticists, archaeologists, linguists, and anthropologists all claim evidence. One model says farming spread mainly as farmers themselves migrated. That is the demic diffusion model. The rival view emphasizes local people adopting new practices.

Craniometric data means careful measurements of skull shape. The authors compared those patterns across early populations. The measurements supported the demic diffusion model. In other words, migrating farmers likely carried agriculture into Europe. The result adds anatomical evidence to a debate often fought with genes and artifacts.
plos-pone-0006847:
Dardo Tomasi and colleagues scanned brains while stomachs were inflated in PLOS ONE in 2009. Gastric distention signals a full stomach during meals. It is a key mechanism controlling food intake. Earlier work showed lower amygdala activation with higher body mass index. Obese subjects seemed to respond differently to fullness signals.

The team associated body mass with brain activation during gastric distention. Differences in response may help explain overeating in obesity. If fullness signals register weakly, meals can run long. The findings carry implications for obesity treatment. They point to brain responses, not just stomach size, as part of the problem.
plos-pone-0006947:
Giovanna Raso, Yuesheng Li, Zhengyuan Zhao, and colleagues mapped a parasitic disease in China in PLOS ONE in 2009. The parasite was Schistosoma japonicum, a blood fluke that infects people. Their study area was the Dongting Lake region of Hunan Province. They built a spatial model of infection rates there.

The model weighed three kinds of influence on infection. These were population traits, animal reservoir hosts, and local environmental factors. The team judged how well each factor could target control work. Maps like theirs help health programs aim treatment and snail control where infections cluster most.
plos-pone-0007047:
David Wunschel, Bobbie-Jo Webb-Robertson, Charles Frevert, and others looked for signs of inhaled germs in PLOS ONE in 2009. Finding proof of exposure to germs in the air could help doctors name an illness fast. Each type of germ may leave its own set of marks in the lung. The team drew fluid washed from the lungs of exposed animals.

They then compared the marks left by each kind of germ. The sets differed enough to tell one exposure from another. Marks like these might one day tell a care team what a sick person breathed in. That would help in outbreaks, in lab mishaps, and in guarding against germ weapons.
plos-pone-0007147:
Stéphane Belin, Anne Beghin, Eduardo Solano-Gonzàlez, and colleagues studied protein factories in breast cancer cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Making protein is a basic task of every cell. Ribosomes do that work, and their own RNA carries chemical activity. Building ribosomes is a complex process with many steps, from gene reading to fine trimming.

The team found this building process goes off balance in breast cancer. The cells' capacity to make protein changed with it. Both shifts tracked with tumor progression. Fast-growing tumors need more protein factories. That need may be a weakness worth targeting with drugs.
plos-pone-0007247:
Kyota Fujita, Toshihiro Seike, Noriko Yutsudo, and colleagues tested hydrogen-rich water in a mouse model of Parkinson disease in 2009. Molecular hydrogen acts as a therapeutic antioxidant in earlier studies. It can buffer oxidative stress, the cell damage linked to brain injury and to Parkinson disease itself.

The authors give mice a toxin that kills dopamine neurons, modeling Parkinson disease. They report that drinking water containing hydrogen reduces dopaminergic neuronal loss. Their PLOS ONE result suggests a simple antioxidant route worth testing further for protecting the brain in this disease.
plos-pone-0007347: Taufiqul Huque, Beverly J. Cowart, Luba Dankulich-Nagrudny, and colleagues reported two people who could not taste sour in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The condition is sour ageusia, a loss of sour taste. Their study concerns sour perception at the front of the tongue. They link the cases to ion channel families called ASIC and PKD, implicating those channels in how humans detect sour tastes.
plos-pone-0007447:
Adimoolam Chandrasekar and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 tracing how modern humans spread into India. Their tool was mitochondrial DNA, the small genome passed from mother to child. They read complete mitochondrial genomes from people carrying one widespread maternal lineage, called macrohaplogroup M. The sample was drawn from a far larger collection of Indian DNA sequences.

Building a family tree from those genomes let them update the known history of lineage M in India. The tree reveals routes and timing for early movement through the South Asian corridor. Such maternal lineages preserve a record of migrations made long before written history. The work adds a detailed genetic map of some of the first human journeys into the region.
plos-pone-0007547:
Claire Watson and Diana Lockwood published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on leprosy in medieval Europe. The disease was common there eight to twelve centuries ago, yet molecular proof was lacking. The team extracted ancient DNA of the leprosy bacterium from medieval bones. They then typed its single-letter variants, the SNPs that mark one strain from another.

The genetic typing confirms the bacterium's identity in the old remains. It also gives insight into the pattern of leprosy across Europe in that era. Ancient DNA turns bones into witnesses of past epidemics. Tracing the strain's family helps explain how the disease spread and faded. The work anchors a disease known from chronicles in hard molecular evidence. It shows archaeology and genetics reading the same page.
plos-pone-0007647:
Jae Lim and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on Zicam, a zinc-based cold remedy sprayed into the nose. Intranasal medicines treat many nasal disorders, but their effects on smell were largely unknown. Zicam, marketed as a homeopathic way to ease cold symptoms, had been implicated in loss of smell by users. The team exposed mouse and human nasal tissue to the product to test those reports directly.

The exposure damaged the nasal tissue that serves smell. Both the animal tissue and the human tissue showed the harm. That laboratory evidence supports the complaints that had gathered around the spray. A remedy applied inside the nose reaches delicate sensory tissue with no protection. The study is an example of bench work answering a consumer safety alarm. It shows a marketed product carrying a risk its label did not suggest.
plos-pone-0007747:
Greta Snellman and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It uses twins to ask how genes shape vitamin D levels. Sunlight and diet are the classic determinants of vitamin D status. Yet together they explain only a modest share of the differences between people.

The team measured blood levels of the main vitamin D marker across seasons. They compared identical and fraternal twins to split genetic from shared influences. Genetic influence turned out to vary with the season. In dark months, genes may matter more because sunlight is scarce. The study refines how vitamin D research should be designed.
plos-pone-0007847:
Niels Halama and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It solves a counting problem in cancer tissue analysis. Doctors increasingly use immune cell counts in tumors to predict outcomes. The counts also help select therapy for individual patients.

Under the microscope, immune cells often clump into tight conglomerates. In a clump, single cells are hard to count accurately. The authors present an approach to estimate cell densities inside such clusters. Their method fits high-throughput analysis of tumor sections. Reliable counts could make immune-based prognosis a routine hospital tool.
plos-pone-0007947:
Krishna Aragam and colleagues compared two sets of heart risk scores in PLOS ONE in 2009. Doctors use the TIMI and GRACE scores to judge risk after chest pain or a heart attack. One set is simpler to work out at the bedside; the other asks for more inputs.

Looking back at patient records, the team checked whether the simpler scores lost any truth. Ease of use matters in a busy ward, but not if it costs sound judgment. Their head-to-head test tells clinics what they give up, or do not give up, when they choose the quicker tool.
plos-pone-0008047:
Sonia Santos and colleagues measured single links in the spinal cord's pain gate in rats for PLOS ONE in 2009. Most pain fibers end in a thin spinal layer where the sorting of pain begins. Small excitatory cells there pass the signals onward, yet their link strengths were unmeasured.

Recording from those cells, the team gauged how strongly each link speaks and how it changes with use. Links that grow or fade with traffic shape which signals reach the brain as pain. The wiring data give drug hunters a sharper picture of where pain can be dialed down.
plos-pone-0008147:
Farhat Khanim and colleagues paired two old drugs against a hard leukemia in PLOS ONE in 2009. Acute myeloid leukemia strikes mostly people over sixty, and standard care fails many of them. The pair joined a cholesterol drug, bezafibrate, with a hormone drug used for other ills.

Together, the two pushed leukemia cells to mature and die in ways neither did alone. Two cheap, well-known drugs with a fresh use would be a gift to older patients who cannot bear harsh chemotherapy. The lab results earned the pair a closer look in trials.
plos-pone-0008247:
Thomas Jubault and colleagues measured brain stem changes in Parkinson's disease in PLOS ONE in 2009. Parkinson's is a neurodegenerative disorder marked by tremor, rigidity, and slowed movement. Diagnosis rests mainly on those motor symptoms. The disease disrupts brain circuits that depend on dopamine. Post-mortem studies had hinted at wider damage, including the brain stem.

Using anatomical MRI, the team detected regional atrophy in the brain stem. Living patients could thus show changes once seen only after death. Imaging such changes may help track the disease earlier. It also broadens the picture of what Parkinson's damages.
plos-pone-0008347:
Antonio Salas and his team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about a harsh brain germ disease. Meningococcal disease is still a top cause of death by germs in rich lands. Two sick people may fare in far apart ways, one mild and one near death. That spread seems to come from host genes mixed with the world round them. The team turned to gene sets passed down in the cell's small power plants.

They asked if these sets, called mitochondrial haplogroups, make some people more prone to the disease. A gene tilt, if real, could flag those most at risk in a surge. It could also show why some cases turn deadly fast. The work adds host genes to the full tale of this disease.
plos-pone-0008447:
Arnon Arazi and co-authors model immune cell interplay in mice in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Regulatory T cells keep the immune system in balance. They help stop attacks on the body's own tissue. More than one subset of these cells exists. But how the subsets affect each other over time was not clear. The authors study CD4 and CD8 regulatory cells.

They track how those cells interact with other T cells in living mice. They look at how numbers rise and fall over time. The work gives a dynamic view, not just a snapshot. It helps explain how immune balance is kept day to day.
plos-pone-0008547:
Yassina Bechah and co-authors hunt for a hidden reservoir of typhus bacteria in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Brill-Zinsser disease is the relapsing form of epidemic typhus. It strikes years or decades after the primary infection. The bacterium is Rickettsia prowazekii. Mechanisms of reactivation and the latency reservoir were poorly understood. The team use a mouse model to find where the bacterium hides.

They show adipose tissue serves as a reservoir for recrudescent infection. Fat tissue shelters the bacterium during its silent years. From there it can re-emerge and cause relapse. Finding the reservoir explains a long-standing mystery of typhus biology.
plos-pone-0008647:
Gemma L. Walmsley, Virginia Arechavala-Gomeza, Marta Fernandez-Fuente, and co-authors published a gene therapy study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It concerns Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a fatal wasting illness striking about one in every three thousand five hundred boys. The cause is missing or faulty dystrophin, a protein muscle fibers need to stay intact. Cavalier King Charles spaniels carry a matching fault.

In those dogs, the team tested exon skipping, which coaxes cells to leave out one faulty gene section. Skipping exon 51 let the gene produce a shorter dystrophin that still worked. Their mutation sits in a known hot spot, yet still responded to the method. That result supports using the same approach against the human disease.
plos-pone-0008747:
Bernhard Singer, Inka Scheffrahn, Robert Kammerer, and colleagues studied sticky surface proteins gone wrong in lung cancer. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The proteins belong to the CEACAM family, which helps cells hold together. Members like CEACAM1 and CEACAM6 shift levels in many human cancers. What those shifts do to cell behavior was poorly known.

In lung adenocarcinoma cells, a scrambled CEACAM pattern drove disorderly growth. Cells lost their mature, organized character. The change hints that adhesion chaos helps tumors grow wildly. Restoring the normal pattern could be a future treatment angle.
plos-pone-0008847:
Lin Miao, Min Wang, Wen-Xuan Yin, and colleagues tested a heart hormone on young heart cells. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Atrial natriuretic peptide is a hormone the heart itself releases. It influences blood pressure and fluid balance in adults. Stem-cell-derived heart cells mimic the embryonic heart in many ways. Whether the hormone tunes their calcium channels early in development was unknown.

The hormone regulated calcium currents in the young cardiomyocytes. Calcium flow drives each heartbeat and much cell signaling. Early tuning may shape how the developing heart wires its rhythm. The result adds a chapter to cardiac development biology.
plos-pone-0008947:
Solomon Conteh and colleagues tested how well malaria germs pass from mosquito to mouse, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lab studies of malaria often inject the germs straight into a vein. Real infection starts with a mosquito bite that leaves the germs in the skin. The team used a mouse form of malaria and a mosquito species that spreads it.

Mosquito bites led to far fewer infections than the needle route did. Even when the mosquitoes carried many germs, passing them on worked poorly. The gap matters because vaccine trials often judge protection using needle shots. Testing through real bites may give a truer picture of how vaccines perform.
plos-pone-0009047:
Enmoore Lin and co-authors compared two malaria species side by side in young Papua New Guinean children, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax share the same villages there. Vivax malaria's burden falls on younger children than falciparum's does. Old malaria-therapy records hinted that immunity to vivax comes faster.

The team tracked infection and illness patterns for both parasites. The two species peaked at different ages and caused different shares of sickness. Faster protection against vivax shaped its place in the age curve. Control programmes in mixed regions must plan for two different diseases, not one.
plos-pone-0009147:
Pin-Tzu Su and co-authors asked why newborn E. coli cells line up so neatly on agar, in PLOS ONE in 2010. When the bacterium divides, its two daughters slide alongside each other. After the first split they sit parallel, like parked cars. An elastic material tethering the cells was the standing explanation.

The team probed what really drives the side-by-side arrangement. Cell shape, wall growth, and surface forces all came under review. Early division patterns seed the layout of whole colonies. Understanding them helps read how bacterial communities organise themselves.
plos-pone-0009247:
Anna Merendino and co-authors published this cancer cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Hsp60 is a helper protein that normally works inside mitochondria, the cell's power stations. In recent years it has also turned up outside cells and on their surfaces. How it gets there, and what it does there, were open questions.

The team showed that human tumor cells actively secrete Hsp60. The protein is not just leaking from dead cells; living cancer cells release it on purpose. That changes how researchers should read Hsp60 found in blood samples. It also raises the question of what signal the released protein sends to nearby tissue.
plos-pone-0009347:
Brooke Snyder and co-authors published this Huntington's disease study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Multipotent stromal cells from bone marrow had shown a surprising talent. Placed in mouse brains, they coaxed the brain's own stem cells to multiply and become neurons. Huntington's disease, which wastes the striatum, was a natural next target.

The team implanted human stromal cells into a transgenic mouse model of Huntington's. The cells increased new neuron formation. They also decreased the shrinkage of the striatum, the region the disease hollows out. Borrowing the brain's own repair crew, rather than replacing tissue, is the strategy this supports.
plos-pone-0009447:
Agnieszka Dyrda and co-authors studied red blood cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. These cells must bend to pass through blood vessels thinner than they are. That bending shapes their membrane and inner frame. The team asked whether a small local dent in the membrane changes the flow of ions across it.

They found that local dents switch on currents that depend on calcium. Currents carried by potassium and by negative ions both rose. The work links the cell's shape changes to its electrical life. That link could matter when red cells stiffen in some blood diseases.
plos-pone-0009547:
Siu-Kin Ng and co-authors mapped a busy stretch of DNA tied to schizophrenia in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gene GABRB2 makes part of a receiver for GABA, the brain's main calming signal. Earlier work showed signs of strong selection in one segment of this gene. That segment holds many single letter variants. The team examined how often DNA shuffles within it.

They found a recombination hotspot, a place where DNA swaps at high rates. Hotspots reshuffle variants into new combinations quickly. In a gene tied to a major mental illness, that churn is notable. It may help explain why this region is both important and hard to pin down.
plos-pone-0009647:
Shahrzad Shirazi Fard and co-authors traced a signal that helps nerves grow in PLOS ONE in 2010. Nerve growth factor tells young neurons to extend branches called neurites. Those branches become the wiring of the nervous system. The signal passes through a chain of proteins inside the cell. The team identified one link, a protein called Tiam1, as a mediator of that growth signal.

Tiam1 helps reorganize the cell's skeleton so a branch can push outward. Without it, the growth response faltered. Filling in this link completes more of the path from signal to shape. The work bears on how nerves repair themselves after injury.
plos-pone-0009747:
Sarcomas are cancers of bone and soft tissue, and they come in many types. Panagiotis Konstantinopoulos and colleagues pooled gene expression data from several sarcoma studies. Their analysis appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Single studies of rare cancers are often small.

Expression data show which genes are switched on in a tumor. Combining datasets let the team test how sarcomas should be classified. The analysis also flagged which cancer pathways were active and which tumors resist chemotherapy. Patterns shared across datasets are likelier to be real and useful. Rare cancers need shared data most.
plos-pone-0009847:
Phytophthora infestans is the water mold behind potato late blight, the Irish famine disease. Roberto Sierra and colleagues hunted for genes the pathogen switches on inside plants. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Late blight still destroys potato crops today.

Genes expressed in planta are active during infection, not in a lab dish. The team mined cDNA libraries, collections of copied gene messages, to discover them. Knowing which genes the pathogen uses inside a host exposes its attack plan. Those genes become targets for resistant crops and new controls.
plos-pone-0009947:
A hospital germ that shrugs off many antibiotics is a growing threat in intensive care. Jung-Jr Ye and colleagues studied patients whose infections changed from treatable to resistant. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The change can happen during a single hospital stay.

The germ is Acinetobacter baumannii, known for multidrug resistance. The patients formerly carried susceptible strains that later appeared as imipenem-resistant strains. Imipenem is a strong antibiotic often held in reserve. Finding the risk factors for that switch helps hospitals stop resistance before it spreads. The patients were treated in hospital wards.
plos-pone-0010147:
The authors were Qingchuan Dong, Ping Meng, Tao Wang, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study tested a small RNA against prostate cancer cells. The RNA, called let-7a, belongs to the microRNA family that fine-tunes gene use. Earlier work found reduced let-7 levels in lung tumors, but its role in prostate cancer was little known.

In lab cultures and in animals, let-7a slowed prostate cancer cell proliferation. It acted by targeting two growth genes, E2F2 and CCND2. Restoring a lost microRNA is one strategy researchers hope to turn into cancer therapy.
plos-pone-0010247:
The authors were Mayte Suárez-Fariñas, Michelle Lowes, Lisa Zaba, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study sought a consistent molecular definition of psoriasis. Several microarray studies had each named genes linked to this skin disease. Lists differed between studies, so the team compared disease genes across all of them, plus their own data.

Using gene set enrichment analysis, they tested which gene patterns truly repeat. A consensus molecular picture can anchor diagnosis and drug research for psoriasis. It also shows how to reconcile gene studies that seem to disagree at first sight.
plos-pone-0010347:
Silvia Goicoechea and co-workers wrote in PLOS ONE in 2010 about palladin, a protein linked to pancreas tumors. Pancreatic cancer is often found late and spreads early, so doctors urgently need early warning signs. Palladin, a protein tied to the cell's inner skeleton, had just emerged as a possible marker. The team asked whether only certain forms of it rise in tumors.

They compared human and mouse pancreatic tumors with healthy tissue. One specific form of palladin was raised in the tumors of both species. A form-specific rise is more useful than a vague one for test design. It could help build blood or tissue tests that flag this cancer sooner. More work would be needed, but the lead is precise.
plos-pone-0010447:
Stefan Prost and a large team read ancient DNA from Arctic lemmings to judge warming's effects, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Global temperature rose modestly over the last 150 years. Even that rise hit the Arctic hardest of all regions. Collared lemmings are small Arctic mammals with a long fossil and subfossil record. Their old bones carry DNA that tracks population change.

Ancient DNA lets scientists watch populations shrink or move across past warm spells. Those records forecast what current warming may do to Arctic species. Lemmings also feed Arctic foxes and owls, so their fate ripples outward. This study turns museum and cave remains into a climate archive. The past, read in genes, becomes a guide to the near future.
plos-pone-0010547:
Paolo Kunderfranco and colleagues showed that ETS family factors switch on a silencing enzyme in prostate cancer in PLOS ONE in 2010. ETS factors guide cell growth and identity in many tissues. They have emerged as key actors in prostate tumors, though their impact was debated. The team traced one path of that impact. It runs through EZH2, an enzyme that chemically silences genes.

Under ETS control, EZH2 silenced a tumor suppressor gene called Nkx3.1. Losing that suppressor frees tumor growth. A chain from factor to enzyme to silenced guard is a satisfying mechanism. It also offers drug points along the chain, including EZH2 itself. The study helps settle what ETS factors really do in this cancer.
plos-pone-0010647:
Klaus Reuter and colleagues solved the structure of an enzyme that helps microbes survive salt, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many microbes make protective compounds when water turns salty. One compound, ectoine, can be upgraded into a stronger form called hydroxyectoine.

The enzyme EctD performs that upgrade, using iron and a partner molecule. The team's crystal structure shows the active site in atomic detail. Key parts grip the iron and position ectoine for the reaction. Knowing the layout helps chemists copy the trick for industry, since these compounds protect proteins and skin in commercial products.
plos-pone-0010747:
Christina Hägglöf and colleagues searched prostate tissue for a sign that predicts survival, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many prostate cancers grow so slowly that treatment harms more than the disease. Doctors still lack sharp tools to tell those men from men who need curative treatment soon.

A receptor called PDGFR-beta was measured in the tissue that supports the tumor, and in healthy prostate tissue. Higher levels tracked with worse survival. The signal sat in support cells, not the cancer cells themselves. A support-tissue marker could help spare low-risk men surgery and radiation they are unlikely to need.
plos-pone-0010847:
Massimo Filippi, Gianna Riccitelli, Andrea Falini and co-authors published this brain imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Empathy shapes how people respond to suffering, and the authors wondered whether diet choices made for ethical reasons come with different brain responses. They compared omnivores with vegetarians and vegans while each group viewed distressing scenes.

Volunteers watched pictures of injured or threatened humans and animals, mixed with calm landscapes, while a scanner recorded brain activity. For human suffering, vegetarians and vegans showed stronger activity in regions tied to emotion and social feeling than omnivores did. Responses to animal suffering differed as well, in a pattern distinct from the human scenes. Filippi and colleagues offer a rare look at how values and daily choices may be reflected in the brain's empathy circuits.
plos-pone-0010947:
Joana Carvalho Moreira de Mello, Érica Sara Souza de Araújo, Raquel Stabellini and co-authors published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Females carry two X chromosomes, so one is switched off in each cell to balance gene dose. In mice, the placenta always silences the father's X, but whether human placenta does the same was disputed, based on very few genes.

The team read allele-specific activity for more than twenty X-linked genes across many placental samples, using natural spelling differences to tell the parents' copies apart. Silencing proved random: either the mother's or the father's X could be off, in a patchwork mosaic. Mello and colleagues settle a long controversy with a broad gene panel. The result shapes how doctors interpret X-linked gene tests done on placental tissue during pregnancy.
plos-pone-0011047:
Miles Scotcher, Luisa Cheng and Larry Stanker published this toxin detection study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Botulinum neurotoxin, the cause of botulism, is among the most potent poisons known and a food safety and biodefense concern. The authors built a sandwich immunoassay for serotype B of the toxin, sensitive enough to detect amounts below the lethal dose in the standard mouse test.

They raised monoclonal antibodies against pieces of the toxin produced in bacteria, then selected the best pairs to capture and flag the toxin in a two-antibody format. The finished assay was applied to detecting the toxin spiked into milk, a realistic contamination scenario. Scotcher and colleagues offer a laboratory test that spares the mouse bioassay, the slow and ethically fraught standard it could replace.
plos-pone-0011147:
Darling, Mau and Perna introduced a genome tool in PLOS ONE in 2010. Comparing whole genomes gets hard once evolution shuffles their blocks, adds genes and drops others. Their program, progressiveMauve, was built to align several genomes despite that mess.

The tool finds shared blocks and tracks how they were rearranged over time. That lets scientists compare related germs and trace how new traits arise. It is useful for studying outbreaks, where small genome changes carry big meaning. A clearer map of genome change also reveals deeper history shared across species.
plos-pone-0011247:
Yuan, Xu, Qi and colleagues studied mouse egg division in PLOS ONE in 2010. For an egg to divide evenly, a spindle must form and grip each chromosome correctly. The team tested a kinase switched on by MAPK signaling for its role in building that spindle in mouse eggs.

The kinase proved required for spindle assembly and for proper attachment between chromosomes and spindle fibers. Without it, eggs risk unequal chromosome counts, a leading cause of failed embryos. Naming required parts aids fertility research. It also helps explain some age related declines in egg quality.
plos-pone-0011347:
Amit Bhardwaj and colleagues studied in 2010 how a hardy enzyme keeps its shape under harsh conditions. The enzyme, a xylanase, breaks down plant fiber, and the family it belongs to is prized for use in industry at high heat. Many proteins have their two ends lying close together, and the team tested whether that contact is a key source of strength.

They altered the contact between the enzyme's start and end sections and watched stability and folding change. Weakening the contact made the protein less able to hold its shape and refold after stress. The result names a simple design rule for tough proteins. Engineers who want enzymes that survive factory heat can build that end-to-end grip in on purpose, rather than finding it by trial and error.
plos-pone-0011447:
Adam Vigil and co-authors mapped the cat immune response to a familiar germ in 2010. Bartonella henselae causes cat scratch disease in people and lives quietly in many cats. To learn which parts of the germ the cat immune system actually targets, the team used protein microarrays, chips carrying many bacterial proteins in tiny spots.

Blood from infected cats lit up a defined set of proteins, charting the antibody response in detail. That chart sharpens diagnosis, since the strongest targets make the best test material. It also matters because this germ bridges pets and people: understanding the cat response helps track how infection persists in its animal host. A better map of feline immunity could eventually support a cat vaccine that cuts human cases at the source.
plos-pone-0011547:
BumChan Park and co-authors showed in 2010 that too much of a cargo protein, or a mutated copy of it, jams the cell's transport system. Optineurin helps move material inside cells along their delivery routes. Faulty optineurin causes some cases of glaucoma, the blinding eye disease, and of ALS, the fatal nerve disease, a pairing that hints at a shared mechanism.

When the team raised optineurin levels or introduced its mutant form, protein trafficking inside the cells was impaired, with cargo failing to reach its destinations on time. One jammed delivery system linking an eye disease and a nerve disease is a powerful clue. It suggests both illnesses may begin, in part, as logistics failures. Drugs that keep cellular traffic moving, or that lower the faulty protein, become rational candidates for two conditions that currently have few.
plos-pone-0011647:
Jixun Dai and co-authors studied an unusual DNA fold in a major cancer gene, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A stretch of the c-MYC promoter, a control region for a gene that drives many cancers, largely governs the gene's activity. One strand of that stretch is rich in the letter C and can fold into a compact form called an I-motif.

The team determined how the main I-motif folds and how stable it is. They found these structures are highly dynamic, shifting shape rather than sitting fixed. A moving target like this may help regulate c-MYC, and it complicates drug designs that aim to lock the fold in place.
plos-pone-0011747:
Marta Nunes and co-authors studied enzymes the malaria parasite sends into its host cell, in PLOS ONE in 2010. To establish infection, the human malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum must remodel the red blood cell it invades. A family of exported enzymes called FIKK kinases, unique to this parasite group, are leading candidates for that remodelling work.

The team showed different family members target distinct components of the red cell membrane. That division of labour reveals a coordinated customisation of the host cell. Each targeted component is a possible weak point for future malaria drugs.
plos-pone-0011847:
Junya Fujimoto and co-authors reported in 2010 on lung tumors in mice exposed to NNK, a cancer-causing chemical found in tobacco. They used mice missing the Gprc5a gene, which normally seems to hold lung tumors back, so the animals develop lung adenocarcinoma after exposure. The study compared gene activity across the whole genome as the disease developed.

That side-by-side comparison highlights which gene networks switch on or off as a tobacco chemical pushes lung tissue toward cancer. Seeing the order and grouping of those changes helps separate early drivers from later side effects. Mouse findings like these give human lung cancer research a set of pathways worth checking in people who smoke or once smoked.
plos-pone-0011947:
Radhika Nair and colleagues set out in 2010 to correct the record on a protein that blocks cell specialization in the breast. The protein, Id1, matters because poorly specialized cells are a hallmark of breast cancer growth. Knowing when and where Id1 normally acts in the mammary gland is basic to understanding when it goes wrong.

The team's findings redefine Id1's expression pattern and its function during mammary development. A corrected baseline changes how earlier cancer findings should be read, since a protein blamed for blocking specialization may have a narrower or different normal job. Careful normal-tissue work of this kind keeps cancer research from chasing artifacts.
plos-pone-0012047:
Kang Ning and Damian Fermin presented in 2010 a method called SAW for finding gene splicing events in RNA sequencing data. Splicing, the editing of gene messages, creates much of the variety in proteins, and new sequencing had produced an extensive profile of it. Finding real splicing events in that flood of reads is not straightforward.

SAW identifies events from splicing fingerprints, the characteristic read patterns a true edit leaves behind. A fingerprint approach can separate genuine edits from sequencing noise at scale. Since faulty splicing underlies many diseases, including cancers, a sharper detector improves every study that reads RNA to find them.
plos-pone-0012147:
Ashok Sharma, Shoshana Bartell, Clifton Baile, and co-authors profiled liver genes in obese mice given leptin, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Leptin is a hormone-like protein that tells the brain to eat less and burn more, and mice that lack it grow severely obese. Giving leptin back causes weight loss, but the liver's part in that response needed mapping.

The team read which liver genes and pathways change as leptin drives the weight off. The liver is the body's chemical clearinghouse, so its switches likely carry much of the effect. A pathway map like this gives obesity research concrete steps to test, instead of treating weight loss as a black box.
plos-pone-0012247:
Aaron Voigt, David Herholz, Fabienne Fiesel, and co-authors tested a nerve-cell protein's role in degeneration using fruit flies, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein, TDP-43, is firmly tied to ALS and to a common form of dementia, where it clumps and misbehaves in nerve cells. Whether the harm comes from the protein's normal job going wrong or from clumping alone was unresolved.

Their in-animal experiments show the protein must be able to bind RNA, its normal working material, for neuron loss to occur. That requirement narrows the search for what exactly kills the neurons. It suggests treatments should target the protein's RNA-handling state, not just clear its clumps.
plos-pone-0012347:
Paul Wikramaratna, Cameron Simmons, Sunetra Gupta and co-authors modeled dengue fever spread in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Dengue comes in four related virus types, and catching one type protects you from that type for life. A second catch with a new type can be worse, yet what third and fourth infections do to outbreaks was far less clear.

Their model tracks how later infections shift the timing and size of epidemics for each virus type. It shows that third and fourth infections, though milder in most people, still feed transmission and help explain dengue's messy, uneven outbreak pattern. The work guides vaccine plans, since a dengue vaccine must handle all four types at once.
plos-pone-0012447:
Nicholas Oesch and Rowland Taylor studied how starburst cells in the retina sense motion direction, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. These cells are where the eye first computes which way things move, but the mechanism was unsettled. The authors tested whether sodium channels that resist the pufferfish toxin tetrodotoxin play a part in that directional response.

The resistant channels did contribute to the cells' directional firing. Each such detail helps complete the wiring diagram of early vision. Knowing how direction is computed in the eye informs both blindness research and the design of artificial vision systems that must detect motion cheaply.
plos-pone-0012547:
Mikhail Rabinovich, Mehmet Muezzinoglu, Irina Strigo and fellow researchers built a math frame for how feelings and thoughts meet in the brain, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The brain is never still; even at rest, its activity moves from state to state in set paths. The team asked if that restless motion, when it goes wrong, could help explain mental illness.

In their frame, a healthy brain moves through its states in a smooth, rich order, while illness narrows or warps the route. One shared math picture lets doctors and scientists compare states as unlike as low mood and split thought. It also gives clear claims that brain scans can test, which is how a bold idea earns its keep.
plos-pone-0012647:
Rydzak, Cotich, Sax and co-authors checked how well a computer model of HIV care matches real life. Such models blend disease data, treatment results and population figures to test care plans before money is spent. Their 2010 paper puts one policy model of HIV and AIDS through a careful audit.

They compared model forecasts with outcomes seen in actual patients and programmes. A model that survives such checks can be trusted to compare drug plans and spending choices. The audit also shows where the model is weakest, guiding the next round of fixes.
plos-pone-0012747:
Uhler, Kumarasamy, Mayer and co-authors weighed the costs and gains of sending TB patients for HIV tests in India. Indian rules already call for referring all TB patients in the highest HIV states. Their 2010 analysis compared routine referral for everyone there with more selective referral.

They counted costs per case found and per life improved under each plan. TB and HIV often arrive together, so joined testing can catch hidden HIV early. Their numbers help a large programme spend limited funds where testing pays most.  The study models costs at the scale of a national programme.
plos-pone-0012847:
Chang, Hsu, Ni and co-authors mapped the boundary between two neighbouring tumour suppressor genes on chromosome 3. RASSF1A and BLU sit head to tail at a spot often lost in cancers. Their 2010 study asked whether the two genes are switched and tagged in step with each other.

They found distinct epigenetic domains split by an insulator bound by CTCF, the genome's boundary protein. Separate domains let the cell control each gene on its own terms. When such boundaries fail in cancer, whole gene neighbourhoods can go wrong at once.
plos-pone-0319447:
Temesegen and colleagues, in a 2026 study, track deaths of young children born to older mothers in Ethiopia. Child survival is a basic marker of a country's development, and Ethiopia carries a heavy share of the global burden, especially among mothers aged thirty-five to forty-nine. The team pooled four national household surveys, from 2000 to 2016.

Deaths before age five fell from well over one hundred per thousand births in 2000 to under sixty in 2016, a real gain. Patterns within that fall matter. Girls, longer gaps between births, some antenatal care, and first births in the thirties all lowered risk. Twin births multiplied risk several times over, as did very large families, births crowded into a few years, and giving birth in the late forties. The authors urge programs that promote birth spacing, pregnancy care, and caution about late pregnancies.
plos-pone-0323847:
Simon Mahler and seven colleagues try to sex chick embryos through the shell in this 2026 study. Knowing sex before hatching matters for farming and for vaccine production in eggs. Their tool images blood flow in the embryo's outer vessels using laser speckle contrast. No opening of the egg is needed. Pictures from over twelve hundred living embryos, three to four days old, trained two deep learning models. The question was whether vessel patterns betray sex.

Honestly, they do not, at least not usefully. Both models scored in the mid-fifties percent, barely above coin-flipping. The results never reached statistical significance at either day. Better cameras or more data might change the answer someday. For now, the study closes a tempting shortcut with proper evidence. Publishing the failure saves hatcheries and laboratories from investing in a method that looks scientific but performs like chance.
plos-pone-0343647:
Simanta Roy led a team of eight authors who studied diabetes care in Bangladesh, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Diabetes drugs work only when patients take them on schedule, and many adults struggle to do so. The team measured which factors track with good or poor adherence among adult patients.

Roy's group found patterns that point to where help can land: reminders, cost relief, and clearer teaching all match gaps the data reveal. Clinics can use such a map to target support rather than scold patients. In Bangladesh, where diabetes is rising fast, better adherence prevents costly complications. The study gives local health planners evidence drawn from their own patient population.
plos-pone-0345347:
Muslim Abbas Syed led a team of four authors setting out a study protocol on AI readiness in Qatar, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Health workers in Qatar's primary care services will meet AI tools in clinics soon, ready or not. The planned mixed methods study will measure AI awareness among these workers and how AI should enter their training.

Syed's protocol maps readiness levels before the technology arrives in force. That timing is smart: training designed after measuring real awareness fits actual gaps, not assumed ones. Primary care is where most patients meet the health system, so its staff's readiness decides whether AI helps or disrupts. Other countries planning AI rollouts can borrow this measure-first approach.
plos-pone-0345847:
Kofi Effah and coauthors published a study in PLOS ONE on a confusing finding in cervical screening in Ghana. Leukoplakia is a white patch on the cervix that the usual vinegar test was not designed to judge. Screening programs in low-resource settings rely on that test, yet nobody knew how often the patch appears or what it means. They reviewed nearly fourteen thousand women, screened by vinegar inspection, mobile colposcopy, or combinations with HPV testing and cytology.

Leukoplakia appeared in just under one percent of women. Almost all showed no whitening on the standard test, so the patch hides from the triage method itself. A minority had an excision procedure, with results from normal to the highest precancer grade. The patch was strongly tied to high-risk HPV and to HIV. High referral dropout and biopsy bottlenecks demand simpler rules and point-of-care triage for such women.
plos-pone-0345947:
Naeemeh Haddadi Esfahani and colleagues tested whether mild brain stimulation helps athletes regain thigh strength after knee ligament surgery. Weak thigh muscles and poor voluntary drive often linger after the operation. Twenty male amateur athletes in early recovery were split by chance. Both groups did standard therapy for ten sessions, with real or sham stimulation added.

Real stimulation used a weak current for twenty minutes per session, while sham faded after thirty seconds, so neither side knew its group. Voluntary drive of the thigh muscle rose clearly with real stimulation, by about seven points more than sham. Raw strength did not differ between groups. Brain help may wake the muscle up, even before strength itself pulls ahead.
plos-pone-0346347:
Drugs that may slow aging itself, nicknamed geroprotectors, are the focus of the REPROGRAM trial described by Daisy Wilson and colleagues. This 2026 PLOS One paper is a protocol, setting out how sixty healthy adults aged seventy and over in England will test three such drugs over three weeks.

Volunteers will receive metformin, fisetin, or spermidine, with blood, fat, and stool samples taken before and after. The main question is whether the drugs cut the number of worn-out, senescent cells in fat tissue. The team will also track inflammation, cell cleanup systems, and gut microbes. No results are reported yet.
plos-pone-0346447:
Solomon Wireko led a team of eight authors tracking tuberculosis trends in northern Ghana, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their records came from a regional referral hospital and covered the years from 2019 to 2024. They counted how often the TB germ was found, and how often it resisted rifampicin, a key drug.

Wireko's group read the six-year pattern year by year. Rising or falling detection can reflect better testing, true changes in spread, or both, and drug resistance trends warn whether standard treatment still works. For Ghana's TB program, a clear local record like this shows where control efforts are gaining ground and where clinics need more support.
plos-pone-0347047:
Qi Fu and Xiaotong Li build a pricing model for financial assets that learns from very fast market data. Older pricing models struggle to keep up with high-frequency trading, where prices move in minutes. Their 2026 study fuses a transformer network, which reads sequences, with a dynamic probability network that links big economic factors to small market moves.

On minute-level data for large Chinese stocks over six years, the fused model priced more accurately than a static version. In simulated trading that charged realistic costs, it earned solid yearly returns with a fair balance of risk. The design keeps some structure visible, so traders can see why prices move rather than trusting a black box blindly.
plos-pone-0347347:
McClaran Shirley and Amber Dawn Stubler measured shells in a museum collection to see how tiny sea snails off Oahu, Hawai'i changed over three decades. Their 2026 paper covers more than fifteen hundred specimens from thirty-seven species, gathered between 1974 and 2007 near Waianae. Most of the snails were smaller than a grain of rice and rarely studied.

For each shell the pair compared weight against length across the collection years. Thirty species showed no clear change over time. Seven species became lighter for their size, a shift that may signal stress as local conditions changed. Because the data come from collected specimens rather than a controlled experiment, the study points to possible vulnerability without proving a cause.
plos-pone-0347547:
Ioannis Karapanos and colleagues interviewed twenty members of a fetal medicine team in East London about breaking unexpected news to pregnant patients, above all those with mental health problems. Scans sometimes reveal serious problems, and how that news is delivered shapes everything after. The group included fetal specialists, newborn doctors, midwives, and specialist nurses.

Five themes emerged, covering helping patients truly understand, offering support, tailoring care to the person, supporting staff themselves, and the weight of inequality. Clear settings, plain words, and involving partners helped; language barriers and low health know-how got in the way. Some clinicians avoided mental health topics for lack of training, and repeated distressing talks took a toll with little formal support. The authors call for training and staff care to match the task's emotional weight.
plos-pone-0347647:
Sophia Gimple and co-workers time the dance between the brain's movement and feeling areas during hand motion. Textbooks cast the feeling area as merely reporting back after movement starts, but that order has been questioned. Their 2026 study uses dense electrode grids placed on the brain surface of patients to compare signal start times in the two areas.

In fast brain signals, the movement area switched on before the feeling area, reliably across participants. Slower signals showed no clear order. Two participants who tried to move with little feedback showed the same fast-signal pattern. The feeling area may help start movement, not just grade it afterward. Such timing maps guide brain-computer tools that read movement intent.
plos-pone-0347747:
Behrouz Ghazi Esfahani, M Elizabeth Stroupe, and co-authors solved the structure of an oversized bacterial enzyme that loads the amino acid methionine onto transfer RNA. The bacterium Mycoplasma penetrans runs a stripped-down genome, yet this enzyme's gene is nearly double the normal size because evolution fused extra domains onto it. Their 2026 study used cryo-electron microscopy to picture the assembled protein.

The enzyme proved to be three fused parts: a mystery domain, a second enzyme that normally works elsewhere in metabolism, and the methionine loader itself. Only the first two parts pair up symmetrically. Modeling suggests the loader section must swing around to accept its transfer RNA partner. The authors discuss whether the unusual assembly lets the parts pass materials directly between them.
plos-pone-0347847:
Shiming Hao proposed a new statistical method in 2026 for judging policy effects from time series when no clean comparison group or helper variable exists. Staggered start dates and hidden influences usually break standard approaches to such questions.

The method leans on a symmetry condition built from a shared stand-in variable to strip out hidden bias. A flexible expansion then supports consistent estimates for several treatments with varied effects. Theory links the estimator's behaviour to a long memory process, and a resampling plan handles the tricky inference. Computer trials suggest the approach works well in the settings it was built for.
plos-pone-0348147:
Henry Techie-Menson and his team tuned a deep learning model that spots sick cocoa pods in photos. Sick pods can ruin a crop if found too late. Most models weigh clues in a fixed order. This one learns a gate that strikes its own mix of two clue types: where a mark sits, and what sort of mark it is.

On a Ghana set, the model hit near ninety-nine per cent right. On three more sets from far spots, it stayed strong. It dipped just on a mixed set of coffee and cocoa. The team calls it a firm tool for farm work where crops are checked by phone or drone.
plos-pone-0348347:
Ambika Kormoker and co-workers lay out a plan for a clinical trial on nerve damage caused by diabetes. The condition dulls feeling in the legs and feet and can lead to serious foot problems. Their 2026 protocol describes a blinded trial in Bangladesh testing gentle nerve-glide therapy, given with mild electric stimulation and home exercises, against a sham version.

Ninety patients will be split evenly between the two groups for twelve sessions across four weeks. Feeling, symptoms, and quality of life will be checked before treatment, right after, and again weeks later. Any harms will be recorded as well. Because the plan is a protocol, it reports no results yet; its value is a careful design for care that avoids adding more drugs.
plos-pone-0348447:
Ratinan Dangwilailert and co-workers test whether a painless light-based finger sensor can judge blood hemoglobin in donors as well as needle tests. Donor screening must catch anemia without wasting willing donors. Their 2026 study at a Bangkok hospital measures three hundred donors three ways: the light sensor, a bedside blood test, and the lab's automatic analyzer.
